[h1] Disclaimer [/h1]
This is not a game for everyone, it has a steep learning curve and many things are not explained to you in-game and require you to use external webtools, read wikis and watch video guides. This is not to say that it's impossible to learn most of the mechanics and inner workings without them, but if you go in blindly expecting to grasp its mechanics all by yourself, you'll have a hard time. With this being said, let's start with the review.


[b] The Galaxy [/b]
The milky way in a true 1:1 scale featuring over 400 billion star systems, many of which have tens or more planets. There are many places to visit, including famous star systems like Alpha Centauri, Sirius, Canis Majoris, our solar system (Sol), etc. The engine that generates the galaxy gets a lot of its data from real world star catalogues, so most systems that are close to the player's start are from real astronomical data, while the vast majority of the rest is procedurally generated. Other than planets and regular stars, there are black holes, neutron stars, white dwarfs and nebulae to see.


[b] Flight Model [/b]
This is something this game does very well, flying in this game is so satisfying and immersive. Learning to fly is not difficult, but simply requires a bit of practice. After a while, flying becomes second nature and you'll see yourself docking and exiting stations all the while boosting and avoiding deadly collisions without dropping a sweat... most of the time anyway. Furthermore, the flight model offers a second mode, where the player has much more control over his ship's movement but disables everything that the flight computer does to correct your rotation and trajectory, resulting is easy loss of control and unwanted spinning if the pilot doesn't understand what he's doing. This is not something I'd recommend for newcomers, and even veterans unless they understand the benefits of it, so stick with flight-assist on.
  
[b] Combat [/b]
Probably one of the most fun activities to do. Combat in this game has probably the most depth of all activities, it's easy to learn but hard to master.
It offers a wide range of weapons, defences and utilities, providing the player with a decent selection of playstyles ranging from simple pulse lasers with unlimited ammo for prolonged fights to high hitting explosives and cannons that shred heavily armored ships at the cost of having limited ammunition. Most weapons have three different versions that further reward players that play better. The best performing weapons have to be aimed manually, while turreted and gimballed weapons offer less punch, but are much easier to use since they automatically track your target.
Although 'bigger is better' is certainly true to some extend when it comes to ship size, even the most skilled pilot in the most expensive ship can lose to a good pilot in a smaller less costly ship.
  

[b]So what do you do in this game?[/b]
You do what you want, really. The freedom is both a gift and a curse of this game, sometimes you lack a direction to go and things to do because unlike other MMOs or games in general, there isn't really a goal to this game unless you make one for yourself. You start small and humble and you make your way up, earn credits, ranks, buy ships, upgrade them, etc.
This game has its flaws, it can be grindy sometimes and 'burnouts' can happen!

There are 3 different 'playstyles' to this game:
[list]
[*] Combat (bounty hunting, assassination missions, joining the war effort, piracy, fighting aliens...)
[*] Trading (passenger transportation, space trucking, mining, smuggling...)
[*] Exploration (discovering planets [and immortalizing your name on them forever], discovering ancient ruins, crashed ships, taking tourists to far away places...)
[/list]
  
[b] The Story [/b]
There is no defined story to progress, not in the traditional sense. There are certain missions that factions can give, but most of them are procedurally generated, so they get stale after a while. Not everything is tied to missions, you are free to do whatever, whenever, there is nothing restricting you to any particular situation or area, if you decide to wander off during a mission you may do so. Other than missions, there are various events that happen in the game, and the whole galaxy follows a certain 'narrative', where minor and major events take place and are usually told through the in-game news organization (GalNet). Which brings me to my next point, background simulation.


[b] Background Simulation (BGS) [/b]
This is the term used for the system that handles the various states that happen to the systems and factions in-game. The BGS handles things like wars, economic status, elections, expansions, civil wars, outbreaks and many more. The BGS can be influenced by players by doing certain activities within that system. For example, if enough players in the same system fight for the side of one warring faction, they can change the tide and make that faction win the war, changing their status and potentially eliminating the other faction from the system. Another example is if players trade a lot, the faction might change state into an economic boom, making it even more profitable to take missions and trade. Player input is not required, as states will organically change with time. These state changes usually take a few days, but can be accelerated with enough players contributing. The BGS is something the average player can safely ignore, as it's a pretty advanced topic, just understanding that factions can be in different states is enough.


[b] Multiplayer [/b]
While this game isn't a true MMO, it's a weird mix of multiplayer and singleplayer. Simply put, there is one shared galaxy between all players on all platforms (even consoles share the same galaxy as PC) and three distinct playmodes: open, private group, solo.
In solo play, you will never see another player directly, you will see NPCs, stations, asteroids and everything else, but not players.
In private group play, everything will be the same with the exception that you can see other players if they were at the exact same place as you [i] and [/i] in the exact same private group. This is usually used when you want to play with friends but want to avoid other players.
In open play, you can see anyone who is also in open, this is essentially one big shared private group.

It should be noted that while the universe is shared between platforms, console players will always only see other console players, and PC players will only see PC players.


[b] Issues with Multiplayer [/b]
This game uses something that's called instancing, and peer to peer connections. There are no traditional servers, which lowers the cost of hosting the game servers, but makes connecting with other players sometimes difficult, especially with dodgy routers that have strict NATs and firewalls. These issues aren't too common, but can happen from time to time.  
Another issue is that, especially in open, there is a limit of how many players can be in the same instance (it's around 15-20 but can be worked around), so a particularly popular place with 100 players will not have everyone see everyone, but rather have them split into 5-10 separate instances where each instance of 10-20 players can only directly interact within the same group of players. It's not like the other players are ghosts, it's just that there are separate 'mini universes' where different things happen at the same time independantly, but again, contribute to the same shared universe.


[b] 'Horizons' Season Pass [/b]
I highly recommend this DLC, as it's featuring many new mechanics and additions that only improve upon the game, if you're planning on exploring a lot (landing on planets), or if you're into PvP and advanced combat (aliens) this is a must buy. Read my review for the DLC [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/cookiesrtasty/recommended/441340/]here[/url].

[b]An awe-inspiring, sometimes frustrating, massively underrated gem.[/b]


I can't recommend this game enough [i]for the right kind of player[/i] - it is definitely not for everyone.

If you're considering buying it, do some research first.  Here's my contribution for your consideration:

You will hate this game if:

- you can't tolerate any bugs (more on this later, but be assured the positives massively outweigh the negatives)
- you want to hop in and be able to do anything well, quickly
- you want to hop from location to location very quickly, ever, even after mastering the controls and in-game tools

...because this is a [b]simulation[/b], not an arcade game.  The developers have gone to great lengths to make this a realistic simulation of being a commander of a ship in a future where humanity has Faster-Than-Light travel.  This has two important consequences:  1) It's complicated - there are a LOT of controls and modes to learn, and the in-game tools have many options, many of which you will need to learn to be effective.  2) Nothing is instant.

For example, say you just bought a new module at an orbital station, and want to go buy an even better one at another station a hundred light years away (and that's a tiny distance by this game's standards!).  Here are the basic steps, all of which occur in real time - there is no fast forward:

Note: You start out with your ship on a landing pad that has been retracted into the interior of the station - you can't use ship outfitting services while your landing pad is not retracted.

1.  Return to surface and launch - you will actually see and hear the landing pad make its way out of the interior of the station before the docking clamps are released.

2.  Navigate out the "keyhole", dodging any interior structures or other craft that are leaving/entering as you are.

3.  Retract landing gear and boost away from the station, until you gain enough distance that "mass lock" turns off.

4.  Open the galaxy map, choose your destination system, and calculate a route.

5.  Start charging your FSD (frame shift drive) in jump mode.

6.  Re-orient your ship so you're pointing at your destination, which may involve moving around or away from obstacles to gain unobstructed line-of-sight.

7.  Accelerate to near max so by the time the FSD is fully charged you're ready to go.  After that there's a four-second countdown before the actual jump.

8.  Wait during the jump itself (while you're traveling several hundred thousand times the speed of light) this will take a few seconds.

9.  Navigate carefully around the star that's right in front of you and very close, being careful not to get too close.  After leaving a jump you're in "supercruise" mode where you can travel hundreds of times the speed of light down to thousands of km/s, but all that change in speed requires time - acceleration is not instant, and is limited by the size and nearness of massive objects (stars, planets, moons, stations).

10. Repeat steps 5 to 9 until you complete all the jumps planned in your route.  Be careful not to restart step 5 until your distance from the star you arrived at is enough to avoid overheating while the FSD charges.  Also be aware that your next jump destination at each jump usually will be initially obstructed by the star you just arrived at, so moving around stars between each jump will be a very common maneuver (close enough to use a fuel-scoop when you get one of those, but not too close that you overheat).

11. Repeat step 6 only, to line up to your destination in the current system.

12. Accelerate, cover the distance, and carefully decelerate when near your destination so you don't overshoot it.

13. At the right time, "safe disengage".  This will pop you out of supercruise within a small enough distance to your destination that you can cover the rest of the distance with normal spaceflight (speeds averaging around 100 to 400 meters per second, depending on your ship, modules, upgrades, power allocation, tonnage of cargo, remaining fuel, etc.).

14. Within a certain # of kilometers, contact the station and request docking.  Do not attempt to enter the keyhole without permission.

15. Navigate to the correct side of the station that has the "keyhole" so you can enter it.  Deploy your landing gear.

16. Carefully enter the keyhole without banging into the sides or crashing into other ships.  This will involve rotating in sync with the rotation of the station until you're far enough in that flight assist will do that for you.

17. Find your assigned landing pad and navigate to it.  If you go to the wrong one you may be fined for loitering (or worse).  Your HUD can help you orient toward it if you don't see it at first.

18. When within a few dozen meters of the landing pad, make sure you are oriented correctly and gently "descend", using the navigation panel to help you tweak your positioning - needs to be just right within a fairly small margin of error - the pad is barely larger than your ship.

19. After landing, enter the station, and use the station services.  Again you will see and hear the landing pad retract into the system.

20. Choose the module you want, buy it, and, if it uses a hard point, watch as the old module retracts and is replaced on your ship.

As you can see, this is decidedly NOT a pick-up-and-play game.  Again, all of this is real time, there is no fast forward, no "fast travel" to avoid any part of this sequence.  With a recent update you can get modules to enable "supercruise assist" and automatic docking/takeoff, but this is only like partial autopilot of a real-world commercial airliner - it only lets you avoid having to do [b]some[/b] of the above manually.  It still occurs in real time and its a good idea to keep paying attention, as problems can occur that the autopilot can't handle, just like in real life.  And step 12 is sometimes a long one - Just do a google search for "Hutton Orbital" and you'll see what I mean.

Now you might wonder why I go into so much detail about what you might hate about a game I wholly recommend.  

Three reasons:

1)  I'd rather spare you the disappointment and aggravation if you're not a good fit for this game.

2)  I'd rather spare the game the down vote if you're just not into this [i]kind[/i] of game.

3)  The realism, complexity, uncompromising difficulty, and exquisite attention to detail are just some of what I and many others absolutely [b]love[/b] about this game.


You will love this game if you:

+ enjoy realistic simulations
+ enjoy mastering a difficult learning curve
+ enjoy any combination of space combat, space trading, space mining, or space exploration
+ want to experience a scale, realistically simulated recreation of the entire Milky Way Galaxy
+ enjoy crisp visuals with extreme attention to realistic detail
+ enjoy phenomenally good, non-stop immersive sound design


And you will absolutely [b]adore[/b] this game if you:

+ Love space.


As for the few negatives, I must say again the game is worth it, but here is a warning for you anyway:

1. Sometimes new players have a very difficult time registering their account or launching the game.  My brother was one who was ready to abandon the game at first, though now it is one of his favorites and he's put in several hundred hours.

2. Sometimes the (incredibly complicated) interface can get confused, and keyboard input starts malfunctioning.  The easiest, always reliable way I've found to solve this is to bind a joystick button to toggle camera view.  A double tap of that button will solve any keyboard difficulty in my experience.

3. Some mission types are known to be broken.  For example, avoid any "massacre infected ____" missions, as you simply cannot complete them currently.  You can usually just abandon these missions with no penalty.


TL;DR - this game is like a diamond: brilliant, with little flaws that ultimately do not overshadow its incredible beauty and value.

I find this a complex and enjoyable game.
It is a bit difficult for my 70 years of age but the concept is wonderful.

A series of rich, deep, and lovingly built simulations with an enormous skill ceiling on piloting. A runaway winner in the field of the most natural feeling deep-space combat and flight, with ship handling varying by the physical position of their thrusters and weapon arcs even varying by their physical position on your ship.

An absolutely unfathomable simulation of the entire Milky Way galaxy that produces breathtaking visuals for explorers and might-as-well-be-infinite variety for those looking to traverse the unknown.

It's an incredible shame that such an unparalleled series of beautiful systems is tacked onto an incredibly uninspired set of mind-numbing gameplay loops, where you can immerse yourself in space combat, mining, or freight for hours to make nearly zero progress toward their outrageously grindy and repetitive objectives. I've never played a game that seems as openly hostile to you enjoying the feeling of progression.

Frontier has a collection of inspired and brilliant engineers and designers with unparalleled technical and tactical vision, but it's unclear whether that ambition left them no time or resources to build robust, interesting, or interconnected gameplay loops, or if they're simply unable to fathom how to make their amazing gameplay lead to any sense of accomplishment or fulfillment.

Odyssey is all of their worst instincts laid bare, especially - xenobiology doesn't even feel done, the shooter plays how you'd expect a shooter built by a flight sim team in a flight sim engine to play, and all of the progression is exactly as mindless, undirected, and soul-crushingly slow as they could make it.

I love Elite and keep coming back to it, but not to play the game they've made, which I hate. Just to explore the world you play it in.

[h1][i]From Cynical Skepticism Blooms Humbling Immersion[/i][/h1]

My first night playing E:D my reaction was one of bleak disappointment.  I’ve learned to manage my expectations of games that come with a lot of hype but that doesn’t always do much to soften the blow, especially when we are dealing with one of my favorite genres.  I kept thinking, “I waited 30 years and paid $60 for Euro Truck in Space? Seriously?”  Unfortunately many players have never moved past this stage. The basic gameplay at first does seem only to consist of navigating menus, watching some warp animations, trying not to crash while trying to park, repeat.

And yet, while I kept repeating this thought to myself, I kept playing.  In fact, the more I played, the more I wanted to keep playing.  At the time I could not identify what was happening.  Shouldn’t I be packing this game up and dismissing it as another instance of hype without substance?

What I realize now is that the game was operating on me on an unconscious level.  Tiny details from every corner of the experience combined with flawless internal consistency to build an emergent narrative structure somewhere inside of me that I was not even aware of until I was already a part of it.  I’ll give you the four examples that, in order, brought me around to recognizing how huge and emergent the E:D universe is and how immersed in it I had already become:

When you request docking clearance at a facility, they give it to you in the form of a spot assignment and a timer.  So there I am trying to park my clanky old VW Rabbit of a spaceship on this backwater industrial platform, scraping it against the walls, generally not succeeding- and the timer runs out.  And I get a communication from the facility.  [i]Move along, your spot is forfeit, you’ve been assessed fines and you won’t be welcome back until they are paid.[/i]

A few hours later, I’m hurtling across a solar system towards a facility orbiting a gas giant.  I’m cruising at maybe and average of 150c.  The planet is between me and the facility and as the gassy behemoth grows in my viewport I notice something- my speed is dropping.  I haven’t throttled down. What the hell?  Several more runs and my suspicions are confirmed: the closer you come to gravitic bodies, the less you are able to break the speed of light. Furthermore, clip too close to a sun and it will anchor you, causing an emergency drop into real space and a seriously life-threatening situation.

Much later, still playing, I’m running a courier mission to a huge station in a densely populated area of the galaxy.  To get to the entrance port I need to fly around to the nightside of beautiful M-class gem...and I notice a twinkle in the corner of my viewport.  I activate head look and turn my gaze that direction.  And there it is.  The nightside of the planet is aglow with a sparkling network of living cities.  It took my breath away.

Here is where things really got serious.  I go online checking supply and demand stats and I make a handful of runs carrying foodstuffs from this certain fringe base just within exploitation radius of the Federation. Well it turns out a lot of other commanders got the same idea, and the base’s food supplies are gutted.  Next thing I know, I’m returning for me- and someone tries to interdict my ship into real space.  Which is terrifying.  I find an escape vector and make it through safely, only to find my scanner alight with “conflict zones.”  Messages start pinging into my comms.  Things like [i]You should not have come back here[/i] and [i]There’s nothing left here except blood[/i] and [i]We won’t let it end this way, we will die free[/i].  When I finally make it to the facility and land,  I find out that a different minor faction unique to the base has taken over operation.  In other words, it would seem, faced with starvation, they staged a coup, and ignited a civil war with the Feds. Incredible.

No one, certainly not the game, explained these things to me.  These are things that I learned about over the course of my journeys.  The game is absolutely rife with these sorts of details: available, amazing, and yet existing without fanfare or gimmick.  They are simply part of the way the universe works.  By the end of these events I realized I had left my Euro Truck impressions far behind.  In fact, I had become thoroughly immersed.  I felt like I was truly sailing the vastness between the stars, one small part of an enormous world- a world far huger than I will ever be, that exists regardless of my interaction.  This recognition was nothing less than humbling.

[h1][i]The Truest RP Experience I’ve Had in a Decade[/i][/h1]

Which brings me to my next point. E:D is not a roleplaying in the sense we usually think of these days.  You accrue reputation levels in various ways, but there are no character stats, skill trees, experience points, or anything like that.  And yet this game is easily the most complete RP I’ve had the pleasure of playing in a very long time.  So how can that be? It happens because the game is almost complete indifferent to the player.

It may seem counterintuitive, but the result is that all meaning has to come from within.  This is no Elder Scrolls, no one is going to tell you you’re here to save the universe.  And to be honest, in the games where someone does say something like that, I don’t feel special.  In fact the RP is largely broken because everyone gets that line. In E:D your decisions are yours alone.  And personally, I have watched CMDR Paklo develop a character organically when faced with the many decisions that are technically easy in game but they are difficult in a subjective moral or ethical sense.  For example, Paklo refuses to participate in the slave trade.  From a practical standpoint slaves are just a number on a spreadsheet in terms of gameplay.  But over time I’ve become invested in Paklo’s path through life- and Paklo will not trade slaves.

The world is emergent in such a way that these sorts of decisions happen on a much larger scale as well.  I’ll give an example. Having become disillusioned with the Federation I recently pledged my fealty to the Imperial Princess Aisling (aka Space Khaleesi), an outspoken critic of the Empire’s historical condoning of the slave trade.  A group of commanders, of their own volition, have banded together at various spots along trade routes known to move slaves.  From these spots they interdict ships, scan their cargo, and if they are carrying slaves, destroy them.  This activity does not occur at the game’s behest.  It is 100% organic roleplaying at its finest.

So to conclude on the merits of the game alone, without addressing Frontier’s business ethics- [b]9.75/10[/b], the highest number rating I have ever given, absolutely essential.

People that expect this to be an action filled space game, [b]don't get this.[/b] 
People that are not willing to invest the time into learning, understanding and mastering this game, [b]don't get this.[/b] 
[b][u]But:[/u][/b]
If you're the Type of Person that can sink more hours into ARMA than COD or drive more in Euro Truck Simulator than in Need for Speed, then this might be a game you can fully enjoy.
[h1] THE GAME [/h1]
The game won't give you anything when launching it for the first time; Expect the bare minimum from the tutorials (but do them anyway), and just go Online to learn from one of the many, dedicated content creators and maybe one of the most helpful and knowledgeableable communities reddit has to offer.
You'll start of with nothing and nowhere to go; There's no (obvious) storyline, no specific mission-to-mission gameplay that  lets you progress, no explanation what would be best to do in your tiny, powerless tincan also reffered to as a Sidewinder, the first standard issue "Ship".
[h1] WHAT TO EXPECT [/h1]
And then again, there lies the beauty of this really rough (but continuesly worked on) gem of a vast and expansive game with whatever you want to do, wherever you might want to go, whoever you want to be. You just got to go for it, grind for it. Grind a lot. 
You want this ship? 
Get the money via missions that might not intrest you. 
You got it, but realized you cant afford the parts you want for e.g exploration? 
Now build it as a Trader and do trading.
Finally it's built up nicely, but you don't want to farm more to be able to afford the insurance?
Watch as you can literally lose all your financial progress in matter of seconds and returning back to the Sidewinder.
[h1] WHAT TO EXPECT 2.0 I GUESS (?) [/h1]
This is not a casual game. If you play, don't expect a time of a game in CS:GO, a short mission is already close to 10 minutes, and obviously has bad pay, so it isn't "worth" the effort.
In fact - Expect to sit and watch system after sytem when you travel far away having to withstand hours of monotony.
Expect not understanding and having to google every second thing you encounter.
Expect being overwhelmed by the amount of controls you have to bind, remember as well as utilize at the right times.
Expect dying from bullies or pirates in ships that you could never match, or "unfair" moments when 5 police ships open fire on you after an accidental shot on them whilst bountyhunting, or a station obliterating you as you get stuck in the entrance.
Expect frustration, time that feels wasted and the weird empty feeling of losing progress in the form of money when you look at the rebuy screen.

[h1] CONCLUSION [/h1]
So, why do i recommend the game?
Back when it had just come out, No Man's Sky seemed so promising but I didn't buy it after the huge backlash of negativity that luckily, since has passed.
And with Star Citizen far away time- and hardwarewise, Elite seemed like the only alternative. And then when you start sinking time into it with nothing else to play, and learning about everything in and around the game, you start loving it. The fact that theres a community called the Fuel Rats, imagine the Fire Department of your city would just save you for free when your car is low on fuel, that A: help and B: teach you about the game while asking for literally nothing, is amazing. Almost everyone i met (outside of comabt zones, but well expect to be shot at they're called that for a reason), was helpful, no intent of trolling, nice in language and behavior, and helpful if you were to drop a quick question or two. Those who would harm you are either people fed up that they didn't inform themselves before buying, or roleplayers who you can chat with and if you play along, these encounters will see you surviving (most likely).
[h1] BEAUTY [/h1]
And not only the astonishing community, but if you're a space nerd (like me), the thrill of actually being the very first person to discover a far away system (which gets very likely the more you move away from the "bubble", the area where most players are as there are 400,000,000,000 Systems), or the way you get pulled in to the game to a point where I personally felt weird when my doorbell rang as I got ripped out of this immersive experience, shaking my body. And this was without VR or a joystick, just in a dark room in front of my usual Setup (I have yet to try either one of them).
[h1] TL;DR [/h1]
So if you're willing to immerse yourself, invest time and most importantly willing to give it a proper chance and not anxiously looking for the <2hr-timestamp, you will find many hours of immersive, technically endless joy and a sense of community and equal intrests that i have never seen in any other MMO.

[h1]Elite Dangerous, a game I've poured hundreds of hours into, and one I have to tell everyone to steer clear away from.[/h1]

The game lures you in with promises of an open world, player driven narrative, an entire galaxy to explore, a wide breadth of ships with countless customization options and so much more. The Galaxy awaits you, so you're told. And while I cannot deny that these features ARE there, hiding beneath that shiny coat of paint lies a rotten bulkhead of a vessel, barely coasting along with the power of false promises, broken mechanics, haphazardly added features, and heaping mountains of technical debt that will ultimately never get resolved. You play the game, get hooked for a bit, realize it's issues, look up and see that the developers recognize those issues, be given false hope that they'll work on resolving them in that magical update that never comes, then watch as they add more content with more issues that follow the same trend. Repeat this for 7 years and you're looking at what we have now.

It's become quite clear to the Elite playerbase that Frontier has no vested interest in fixing this game or it's problems, slapping the occasional bandage on it's open wounds and giving them a treat to remind them that they're there and they care, only to leave it abandoned again to fend for itself. The recent release of Elite Dangerous: Odyssey, further cements this problem. A full $60 priced, broken, unfinished alpha of an expansion that completely wrecked this game and removed tons of features, while not delivering on features players have been wanting for years, has completely killed not only any hopes that players had that this game might get fixed, but also it's playerbase. The playerbase, once thriving into the 20k+ range, has plummeted into the 4k's, and is continuing to slide downwards.

Player interaction is almost non-existent beyond staring at your buddies ship to take screenshots or playing space murderhobo, despite this game being a online space MMO. The games famed background economic simulation has ground to an absolute standstill. The vast majority of player activities simply do not pay well, and are almost never worth the hassle, and the ones that are, are easily the safest, most boring jobs in the galaxy. Combat balance is also completely out the window and has been since the Horizons Expansion. The PvP scene is dominated by either griefers roaming in squads of the largest ships with shields so minmaxed to the extreme that only extremely niche, dedicated vessels that no casual player would dedicate time to building can counter them, or by people rocking turbo-fast and agile ships with alpha-strike builds looking to sealclub newbies who can't fight back. The grind for this game is beyond abysmal, boring, uninvolved, and so tedious that a majority of players just resort to googling the best places to grind materials... I could literally spend hours writing a multi page thesis on everything wrong with the game, but I'm just going to move on. In 2019, Frontier all but abandoned the game while their "A crew" of developers went off to work on Elite Dangerous: Odyssey.  We were left with one small content update, fleet carriers, as well as an in-game monetary system named "Arx" used for purchasing cosmetics, rather than a straight cash-for-cosmetics exchange. We were told, though, that Odyssey was going to be amazing. 
Elite Dangerous was one of the top VR games, with a deep, slow-burn lore, an immersive experience, and walked a clumsy line between realism and gameplay.  People invested hundreds of dollars, if not more, in HOTAS setups, VR equipment, and custom made gaming chairs for Elite Dangerous.  It was a space flight simulator. 
In mid-2021, after several delays, Frontier released Odyssey.  There was nothing new on the space sim front except a lighting change that made everything dark and hard to see.  Much of what took place needed to be done with night vision on, which meant that it was impossible to enjoy the lighting and textures because all you could see was green.  Unless, of course, you were on a planet's surface, and in the dark, where all you had was a flashlight because night vision was stuck behind the same kind of grind they'd worked to eliminate in the Beyond days. The promises that were made along the way, from game performance to game expectations, were all lies.

You should not buy this game.  There are other games that do what Elite Dangerous has pivoted to try to do, and those games do it better.

Elite offers the player several journeys. I will describe these journeys and let the readers consider for themselves. Sadly I cannot vote 'neutral' or I would do that. 

Journey into random

Following the original experiment of Elite (1984), Frontier Developments (FD) have taken up the challenge to make an essentially infinite universe. There is just a little problem. How do you make an infinite universe with a finite work force? The answer is the random generator. These things can spew out endless, uninteresting permutations of planetary systems. The result is just noise masqueraded in another way. Many developers have given up this approach in favour of designed universes. FD have chosen to solder on and mix non-random easter eggs in. Yet, you take some random station or system. The experience has the perceptual feeling of just having been sampled from the same bowl of soup. Sometimes your spoon catches a potato, sometimes an onion. You can tell its all from the same chef, Le Generateur.

Journey into disconnect

Elite's random universe is a sandbox. Players can scan planets and systems, transport or smuggle cargo and passengers, mine resources, and fight. You can do missions which are just text wrappers of those tasks. On top of these microscale activities there are some constructs that try to bring some cohesion to the whole. These are powerplay, galactic storyline, community events and thargoids. The reader can find details elsewhere. The key observation is that they matter very little to any of the things you do as a player. It does not matter much which faction controls the system. It does not matter what the galactic news say today. You don't need to read them. Community events stay internal to the systems in question. It does not matter there is a new dangerous existential space threat: The Thargoids! During my hundreds hours of gameplay, I never saw a single one. I did not go look for them. 

What I mean by saying these things don't matter is that a station will always have 180 tons of wine for you to transport, or some criminal to bounty hunt. If not, there will always be another station that will. There will always be planets to scan. The conflict zones will have endless skirmishes, the resource extraction zones will have miners and pirates. Police ships will patrol around, business as usual. The endless universe is very robust. Something goes bust, you move on, more of the same will await you elsewhere. You don't have to care what 'meaningful' structure FD tries to add on top of the random generated world. It does not connect, it affects only a little, and almost only when you seek it.

Elite Dangerous is an online multiplayer game. Another aspect of disconnect comes from the game allowing you to choose between open and solo playing instances. In solo, you cannot meet other players. The open is a more dangerous place due to the murderous habits of the other people. Unfortunately the game provides absolutely zero in-game reward for playing in the open (that I know of). You just get more risk, but no more reward, unless you consider the risk itself as a reward. This is not a great economic incentive, leading many players doubtlessly to play solo and leave the open to the pvp experts to prey on each other. 

But finally something connects! The economic system! It connects between open and solo, with a wonderful consequence that even powerplay can be entirely done in solo. You can undermine other factions, fortify your own, all from the cozy safety of your solo bubble. And so can they. All this fighting without ever meeting. Your numeric amount of toil against theirs is what matters. The tally is taken every Thursday morning.

Journey into grind

While learning how the game works, what is there to do and see, you get pulled into the grind. You choose some activity and try it out. If its mining, bounty hunting, scanning planets, or whatever, you realize your beginning equipment is crummy for that. You do these tasks and earn credits and get better equipment that helps with the tasks. To earn credits, you grind these tasks, on and on. You repeat the same motions endlessly, sometimes even mindlessly. You can easily do missions and chat on the phone at the same time. Many activities are about as challenging as being a cash register operator, only demanding less attention. Instead, what they demand is time. Elite is a massive time sink. No quick transportation (for players!). No quick credits. No quick rank.

I arrived to the game when the golden days had already passed. Every exploit... ahem, good way to earn, had been already "nerfed". The wonderful "massacre mission stacking", "long range cargo missions", and paradise-like systems for gaining navy rank -- long gone. I read accounts of taking down massive Anacondas with your starting Sidewinder. Ancient history. Now the game appears tuned so that you need to buy the Horizons expansion to be competitive with the higher ranked enemies. Mind you, you can't still pay to win: once you have the expansion, you have to grind more to obtain its randomly generated benefits: the "engineered" equipment might not turn out so good. Then you can grind retries.

As the game does not require you to play in open, nor does it require you to pay a monthly fee, why is 'advancement' put behind such massive grind? Who benefits from this? Is it simply to keep the players around long enough for the next expansion which is then sold by "nerfing" the previous mechanics instead of pure content-appeal? Or does somebody enjoy the grind? It does have meditative qualities.

Journey into nihilism

Finally you're at the top of the foodchain (or your grind tolerance). You have amassed money, ships and titles. What do you do with these? The ships fly and perform a bit differently. The titles are just orange text on a black background. It says somewhere you're a Rear Admiral or a Duke. They forget to mention you earned these honorary titles by donations and being a postman. As a duke, you have no militia, no fleets or command, no property, no income, no political prestige, and no invitations to galas with creme de la creme. What being a duke gives you is the permission to grind yourself a ship called 'Cutter' and the next title.

Your net worth is just a number. Oh, you can splurge with it, buy a cargo hold full of narcotics or slaves. You cannot enjoy these goods yourself. These are represented in the game only as text. In Elite Dangerous, I've never seen a coin, a slave, or an enticing powder trail on a glass table. With his slaves, Jabba of the 80s gets more eye-candy and fanservice than players of Elite in 2017.

In the end the emptiness of all your endeavours is clear. There is no reward inside the game. Whatever love, happiness, gratification and sense of achievement there is, is all outside the screen, in you. When you look at the Elite spreadsheet of your billions and the list of your titles, do you feel happy? Or do you feel you have wasted the hours, done it all for nothing? The journey has showed you the universe and your place in it. You are an unimportant, meaningless speckle of random stardust in a random world, repeating the motions. The only mark you may leave is your name as the first discoverer of some random system.

Shutting Elite Dangerous and taking a step back, I wonder of the lessons of its futile journeys, how much they resemble our everyday life. We all know the drill: the randomness of it all (the blind watchmaker!), the pointless grind, the maintenance of existence. The pointless net worths, pointless titles, surrounded by pointless material possessions. When you have it all, what is it good for? Do you know?

Are we still in the game?

The game is perfectly controllable with keyboard and mouse, just make sure to change the default setting, which are useless. This guide helped me a lot:

Elite: Dangerous is a shining example of how [u][b]not[/b][/u] to do game development. Elite is, at its core, actually a great game - I wouldn't have so many hours in it if it didn't have a kernel of goodness in there somewhere.

The TL;DR is that Elite has [i]some[/i] value, but despite having the appearance of life, the game's development is hollow. Features get added but are tacked on to the game as an afterthought rather than integrated seamlessly; shiny new objects are introduced and then ignored thanks to being useless in actual gameplay; and factions within the community shriek for mutually exclusive and generally ill-conceived changes that may or may not ever be answered. Odyssey came with new gameplay, but also quite literally divided the community between DLC and no DLC game modes, and also arrived with a host of bugs, performance problems, graphical changes, and an inferior UI redesign that all degraded Elite's strong point of excellent presentation.

I [b]hate it[/b] when people knee-jerk cry "DEAD GAME" in response to the slightest downturn in popularity or controversial change, but with Elite while I don't think the game is dead, it's certainly not healthy, and Frontier's mismanagement of the game's update cycle for the past 5 years or so have thoroughly convinced me that the game's growth is horribly stunted.

It's not dead (yet)
It's not unplayable
It's even fun
But it could be so, so much more.


On the positive side, Elite:
- Has an excellent flight model with great variation between ships and a staggeringly high skill ceiling. Pilot skill matters, and when you're flying well you can FEEL it.
- Has superb visual and audio design. The artists for this game consistently knock it out of the park - audio and visual feedback is strong, the environments are beautiful, and ships and weapons look great and are highly detailed.

The basic fundamentals of "fly around and look at/shoot at stuff" are rock-solid.
It's everything around that core that suffers - and the sad thing is that most of the flaws work to negate other potentially good features of the game. More infuriating is that many of these issues could be fixed or at least mitigated with minimal effort from the developers, yet basic problems frequently persist for years without even an attempt at a fix.


On the negative side, Elite:
- Has serious problems with grindy "gameplay" in a game which is NOT a F2P MMO trying to sell you a subscription. Most interactions with the game world are "do X but a lot" - hauling lots of cargo, killing lots of enemies, traveling a long distance, gathering a lot of materials. The mundane, repetitive nature of the core gameplay loops make the game lose its charm after the initial glory of the audiovisual presentation wears off.

- Has persistent balance problems with ship outfitting where a large fraction of the available weapons, modules, upgrades, and even some ships are clearly inferior to alternatives or simply bad for no good reason. This is especially sad in the case of the unlockable weapons, which look and sound amazing but are generally let down by stats inferior to more mundane alternatives. Many of the balance issues stand out glaringly when you take any sort of time to compare options, and most could be fixed in minutes with some simple stat tweaks.

- Has poorly implemented multiplayer, combining the inconsistency of peer to peer and the always-online requirements of servers. All player-player interaction is done through peer-to-peer, but the game still uses servers to handle missions and the game world economics etc.

- Has co-op which is either generally fine except for buggy behavior thanks to P2P networking (Wings) or is cool but functionally inferior to and mutually exclusive with wing co-op (Multicrew)

- Has terrible PvP systems; with an "Arena" mode that's more or less entirely detached from the rest of the game and revolves around stealing kills and/or overpowered powerups in Arena-exclusive ships instead of your normal one; "Powerplay", which is an opt-in faction warfare system engineered to be a logistics race that can never have a winner; and a laughable "crime and punishment" system that, as the name suggests, is more tailored to try and make life miserable for anyone who tries to engage with any of the game's criminal options than it is to creating an interesting "sheriff/outlaw" dynamic.

- Has poor tutorials which do little to soften the game's steep learning curve by failing to tell new players about critical game mechanics and encouraging them to crutch on autopilot functions. The main tutorial, for example, completely locks the player out of any of their lateral/vertical thrust inputs and prevents them from adjusting power distribution, which are two of the most essential parts of piloting. It fails to even suggest that they might be used, or what they do (lateral/vertical thrust are essential for any kind of positioning, from combat to landing, and distributor management is the core resource management for flying that, when done right, basically doubles your ship's performance)

- Has poor documentation of features overall; statistics and descriptions of how game elements function are often buried in menus, are completely missing, or are labeled [i]falsely[/i] when an item receives a change but not its description. If you want to understand how anything works or even find something you want, you'll need an online resource or you'll be fumbling around in the dark.

- Has an incredible number of "noob traps" thanks to the low quality of the tutorials, in-game information, and overall balance. Classic examples include beam lasers (which have an attractively high DPS stat, but are incredibly inefficient and will suck your power dry if not accounted for) and the Fast Boot FSD modification, which sounds like it reduces the your cooldown between jumps, but actually simply makes the FSD turn on faster after having power cut, which is entirely separate and significantly less useful.

- Has poor NPC balance; thanks to grindy combat missions demanding the slaughter of mass numbers of enemy ships, community complaints about difficulty (justified or not), and the developers' seeming inability to understand minmaxing in their own game, NPCs are generally either poorly equipped, dumb as dirt pushovers, or better equipped but usually incoherently built (thanks, outfitting noob traps!) and still dumb. Outside of the early game where the player is flying around in a tiny ship made of paper, NPCs almost completely cease to be a threat once a player accumulates a significant amount of engineering upgrades with a good build.

- Has problems with its progression systems and resource collection strongly incentivizing or outright demanding metagaming in order to progress. "Personal narrative" takes a back seat when you must go run some errand in order to unlock an item or gather resources you need to do what you [b]actually[/b] want to. The engineering upgrade system in particular requires a lot of miscellaneous errands to unlock things and gather resources, and while I can understand the variety of requirements being an encouragement to try other sides of the game, it often makes the game into a decision between "Do I want to have fun with something I like?" and "Do I want to progress doing something I hate?"

- Has a LOT of dead time. There is a place for quiet, for a moment of rest for pacing reasons, but Elite crosses the line into busy work and tedium. Even if you're looking for a chill space trucking experience, repetition and the clunky UI get old eventually. The economic side of things is also decent but not exceptional, so if you're looking for deeper trading simulation, Elite isn't the place for it.


Ironically, the obscurity of the game mechanics has been a major factor in why I stuck around, but eventually you run out of bottom of the barrel to scrape up. I got my money's worth, for sure, but I didn't get my time's worth.

Title: 81 hours in and I finally get it

Rating: Recommended

Hours Played: 81.0 hrs

I am 54 years old. I have been playing video games since the late 70s. I have seen every space game come and go, from Elite on the BBC Micro to Star Citizen's never-ending crowdfunding campaign. So when I say this game surprised me, I mean it.

I bought Elite Dangerous on a sale with low expectations. I thought it would be pretty but shallow. And for the first 10 hours, I wasn't sure. The learning curve is a wall. The tutorials are basic. The game throws you into a Sidewinder and basically says "good luck." But I stuck with it because something felt right. The way the ship moved. The hum of the reactor. The sheer silence when you cut throttle in deep space.

Now at 81 hours, I am hooked. Not in a frantic, addicted way. In a slow, comfortable way. Like learning to sail or flying a small plane. You get better because you have to. The game does not hold your hand and that is a relief at my age. I am tired of waypoints and quest markers and NPCs telling me I am the chosen one. Here, you are nobody. Just a pilot with a loaned ship and a galaxy to figure out.

Let me break down why this works for me.

The sound design is the best I have ever heard. And I have heard a lot. The frame shift drive charging up never gets old. The way your canopy cracks when you get too close to a star. The computer voice telling you about a planetary scan. It all feels physical. Like you are inside a machine that has weight and risk. Play with good headphones. Do not skip this.

The scale is not a gimmick. It is a tool. When you fly 200,000 light seconds to a station, that is not a loading screen. That is you committing to the trip. You check your phone. You make a cup of tea. You watch the star get bigger and bigger until it fills your whole screen. It forces you to slow down. At my age, I appreciate that more than I expected.

The grind is real but people misunderstand it. Yes, it takes a long time to get the big ships. But here is the thing. If you only care about the Anaconda, you will burn out and hate the game. If you care about the journey, about running trade routes, about dodging pirates, about that one time you barely made it through the mail slot with no shields and 10 seconds of air left, then the grind is just the story you are living. I have a Caspian Explorer now. It took me 70 hours. I earned every credit and I remember most of the trips that got me there.

Who should buy this?
Buy it if you like games that expect something from you. Buy it if you ever looked up at the night sky and felt small in a good way. Buy it if you do not need constant explosions and cutscenes to stay interested.

Do not buy it if you need action every five minutes. Do not buy it if you hate reading third party websites. Because yes, you will need Inara and EDDB and a few other tools outside the game. That is just how it works. It is not a flaw. It is part of the experience.

I have not seen the aliens yet. I have not engineered a single module. I have only visited maybe 200 systems out of 400 billion. And I still feel like I got my money's worth. That is rare for a game these days.

If you are on the fence, wait for a sale if you want. But buy it. Give it time. Let it teach you its rhythm. It is not for everyone. But if it is for you, it will stick with you for a long time.

One last thing. The audio team deserves some kind of award. I do not say that lightly.

[h2]This used to be my dream game.[/h2]
When I first launched it on a laptop that I wasn't sure could handle it, I literally teared up. I was always a fan of space, space exploration and games that could fulfill that dream at least to some extent. I was also a huge fan of the older Elite games, I spent probably hundreds of hours in them.
The incredibly vast, realistic galaxy that you can just fly off to, away from civilization, to potentially find something cool, was all I was dreaming about in a game.

[h3]Sadly, there was nothing to be found there.[/h3]
Outside of the Bubble, a.k.a. human inhabited space, there was basically nothing to do. Barren, boring rocks everywhere, and every planet that could be somewhat interesting to explore is to this day unavailable for landing. An earth-like world, a world like Titan with heavy atmosperes and methane rivers, a volcanic world with erupting volcanoes and shaking ground...
You will see nothing like that in this game. Everything is barren, barren and boring. They tried to add some life form scanning, but in the end it also came down to spreadsheets and optimizations, which planets are more likely to have the most expensive life forms to scan. And those life forms are static and boring as well. I don't even know how something can grow on a planet with no ecosystem, no sustenance and barely any atmosphere. This whole system doesn't make any godd*mn sense.

[h3]The devs are just NOT listening to the community. Like, at all.[/h3]
For literal YEARS players asked for SPECIFIC things to be implemented into this game.
Things like ship interiors that you can walk around in. We barely care about even being able to do something there, just give us the interiors!
But for many years it's been just Thargoids. Thargoids, Thargoids, Thargoids. I got sick of that word in the end, even though at first they seemed mysterious, spooky and intriguing.
The devs KEEP focusing on the Bubble content, keep changing systems that will keep the players in the Bubble, when they have a gigantic, life-size galaxy with hundreds of billions of stars that have NOTHING to go there for outside of occasional sight-seeing, and even then it gets old pretty fast.
I dreamed of exploring the galaxy in this game, but in the end I turned around half-way each time I settled out to go for a trip into the unknown. It was boring and monotonous. [b]There is nothing there.[/b]

[h3]Some systems and mechanics are just made to waste your time and make the game more grindy.[/h3]
The biggest doodoo among them being the outfitting system. [b]WHY IN NINE HELLS do we have to randomly fly from base to base, with no database being in the game, in search for a specific module, unless we use a third party database in the browser?[/b]
Honestly, just f*** you for this one, FDev. Same goes for having to return to the terminal in the system you picked up a mission from after you finished it. Like, what the f***? WHY?!
Yes, there are superpower Fleet Carriers now, but that's besides the point. 
There are lore-based technologies in the game that allow instant communication between players hundreds and thousands of light years away from each other, you receive galaxy news, you can purchase a system's information while being far away, but no, an in-game database on commodities and modules is somehow not implemented just for you to either stumble around aimlessly, or use an out-of-the-game resource. This is dumb.

[h3]And finally, the sort-of scummy monetization politics.[/h3]
FDev in their infinite wisdom, decided to paywall any new ships they release for several months.
'Nuff said. That is just dirty. I know you have to maintain the servers and keep the development, but when you don't actually listen to your community and then you do something like this, even most die-hard fans can lose faith. I like it... but it has both pros and cons. It is more a space sandbox than a [i]game[/i].

The immersion is amazing and it really makes you feel like some kind of space pirate/cowboy/mercenary. You do have the freedom to go anywhere, to configure your ship however you like, to ally or make enemy with any of the factions, and to run any missions you choose. You have the entire galaxy at your disposal to bounty hunt, pirate, explore, mine, trade, taxi, wage war, or whatever else you like. The atmosphere and audiovisual experience is spot on; everything contributes to making feel like you're actually alone in a tin can floating in the void of space. The ship's computer, the vistas of space, the music and notifications when docking/undocking, jumping into witchspace, flying to and landing on a planet, the dread of arriving close to a neutron star, having the menus being managed through the ship's interface - that's all awesome. The flight and combat mechanics are also very good (with flight controllers).

The distances and travel times are... interesting. You must physically go everywhere you need to interact and there is no fast-travel, so planning your itinerary, ship modules, refuelling points, and then travelling there is most of the game. You really don't want to spend half the night jumping somewhere just to realise you forgot to bring a module and need to go back (but it happens). You'll become familiar with your ships and even learn a few things about stars and KGBFOAM. The fact that the map is our own Milky Way galaxy lets you visit almost any location mentioned in space documentaries - which is also kinda cool. The ships are very well balanced and while there are a few favorites, none of them is "the best"; it always boils down to what you want out of it. You can try the ships for cheap (95% sellback) and they are all available to ingame credits - no microtransactions required.

On the downside... it requires a big commitment and only offers an ocean deep as a puddle. Virtually everything is procedurally generated (size oblige), so anywhere you go is kinda more of the same - but there's still hundreds of hours of new experiences before you've seen everything it has to offer. The game(spaceports) menus are also a bit tedious to navigate, which makes refitting an entire fleet kind of a logistical headache.

There's a severe lack of information; the tutorial teaches you nothing, and many players probably give up before they complete their first docking. It doesn't get any better and you will be forced to use several guides and external resources just to go by (Inara, Coriolis, EDCoPilot, etc). You'll have to learn everything on your own: the ships and their pages of statistics, the modules and their classification, the ships' interface, the power configurations, the different engines/drives/speeds, the scans and scanmodes, the limpet drones and cargo management, how to use the map, how to use rovers and fighters, factions, powerplays, ranks, how to fly, how to dock/undock, how to fight, all about weapons, the space suits and customizations, everything about engineering and materials (yikes). The game doesn't even tell you about what activities are out there or what you need to run a mission; nothing. [i]Everything[/i] needs to be figured out by yourself... but it is rewarding once you do, and it all contributes to the feeling of being just one Commander trying to make it in a vast, dynamic universe.

[b]TL;DR:[/b] It is an amazing space sandbox to get lost into - but it is very much not a casual game that you can just pick-and-play. You have to commit to learn how to get something out of it. It is exactly what [i]I[/i] wanted it to be so I do recommend it - but only if that's the experience that you're looking for.

Elite: Dangerous is a simulator: it simulates the Milky Way galaxy (shared by players) on a 1:1 scale, and it simulates space ships flying through said galaxy, commandeered by you.
Let me start by saying Elite: Dangerous isn't for everyone, but also lots of people just never realize this might well be for them. It has a pretty steep learning curve and it doesn't hold your hand or gently guide you, although there are training missions, and the game starts with a decent tutorial that covers some of the most important aspects of the game. But not everything. A lot (and I mean a LOT) is left for you to discover. This doesn't have to be a show stopper: there are excellent fan-made tools that add to the game, and there is lots of information that can help you understand the game.

Another aspect that can be a deal-breaker is the lack of a campaign. Once you've finished the tutorials, the game kicks you out of the nest and releases you into the wild. But it expects nothing from you. You can sit at the a bar for the rest of eternity if you like. Elite won't stop you, and it won't judge you. You have to make your own game, pick your own path and do whatever sounds like fun to you. There's a good variety of game play loops to spend time on. There are lots of goals that you can set for yourself, but you must set them because the game will not, just like you will never be that one hero that saved the galaxy.

There are several reasons why I love Elite: Dangerous myself. For one, it doesn't ask anything of me, and I can set a pace for myself. Any pace is a good pace. Also, it can be incredibly pretty. 
I like to play the cockpit parts of the game in VR, which is one of the most incredible experiences I've had in VR. It's also just fun to fly a ship, in the same way it can be fun to drive and operate a car. 

BTW, you can visit the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way.

I put in my info, then I was taken to a chat forum where REAL PLAYERS asked me about my situation. They gave me some instructions, and before I knew it, two players found me in the emptiness I was stranded in. They gave me fuel, and directed me to the nearest starport. It was still kinda far from my position, but the fuel they gave me got me there, where I bought a crucial item that every explorer needs- 
A fuel scoop, which you can use to harvest fuel from solar gas giants WITHOUT going to a starport.
Overall, the community in this game is GREAT. And even though I know that player pirates are out there somewhere, they're not as prevalent as NPC pirates. Most players are just doing their jobs and having fun exploring this HUMONGOUS game. 

I'M NOT FREAKING JOKING. THIS IS THE BIGGEST OPEN GALAXY GAME I'VE EVER SEEN. There's absolutely NO WAY you can go from one end of the game to the other in a single real-time day, And at the time of me writing this, I've played 35 hours of this, and I haven't even discovered a full 1% of what's out there. But I'm really excited to see everything.
Every journey takes preparation and careful planning as you go. 
Which is why it's so scary when something bad actually happens. In my case, I was completely and utterly ALONE. I didn't even have the comfort of the NPCs because they don't venture into places where starports aren't present. But you know who does? THARGOIDS.

Wanna be a bounty hunter who hunts down wanted pirates, both Players and NPCs? You can do it.
Wanna be a space miner who collects and sells as many rare metals and minerals as possible? You can do it.
Wanna be a black market smuggler who carries illicit cargo right under the noses of the law? You can do it.

There's a bunch of career paths that you can get into, and none of them are inaccessible from the very beginning, because they go by a recommended skill level list. If you do one of those mission types listed above, you'll gain experience and a reputation from it, which allows you to move forward in that career.
You can earn money really quick in this game by doing a bunch of stuff, or buy doing the same thing over and over again. It's literally carving your path into the galaxy.

With more than 1500 hours in this game, I feel that I am qualified to leave a review. I should probably stipulate this with the fact that I focus solely one aspect of Elite and eschew every other- that is, exploration.

I have no opinion of the combat system, trading engines, background simulations, or anti-xeno activities. None of the storyline means much to me, but that is because the action that is occupying most of the active galaxy is far beyond me, 10's of thousands of light years, in fact.

I am an explorer. I find new things that no other human has ever seen before. It is the crux of my existence, the reason that I am out in space in the first place. My rush comes from being the first person to ever set foot on a planet, the first person to see a massive star, or the first observer of a particular black hole. When I go into a new system, I don't know what's there, and it takes a bit of effort to find out what is. Most of the time it's nothing special, a bunch of ice balls orbiting a small run-of-the-mill red dwarf star. But occasionally, there's magic.

A tightly orbiting pair of binary planets, a 5-star system all orbiting within a few light seconds of each other, a glowing green gas giant. Needles in the proverbial haystack, but that's what I'm very good at- finding needles. It requires time and patience, and the sense of being far across the galaxy and distant from all of the woes of humanity is one that keeps me coming back. I have my own fleet carrier that acts as a mobile base and gives me a place to call home. I don't need to find a station, I brought mine with me.

And then there's the universe itself. All of those stars are things I've read about in books as a kid and as an astronomy nerd. I get to geek out over how crazy fast some planets orbits can be, or land on a moon that rotates as fast as the engine can handle. Watching a planet rise over the horizon of an orbiting moon in real time is amazing to experience, and so far not a single other game has provided me with the sense of wonder that Elite does frequently. There are distant stars in the sky and not a single constellation that I know, but if I want to I can visit every single point of light in that night sky, and in the end they're mine. Chances are no one else will ever see the stars I explore, or the planets I discover, unless I decide to tell them about it.

The Thargoids can have humanity- But they can't take the sky from me.

How to enjoy Elite Dangerous:

- Understand that the concept is a space sandbox, and don't expect any hand holding
- Set your own goals
- Embrace the in game community. Players are some of the friendliest I've ever met in online gaming. o7
- Ignore the forums
- Don't grind.

How not to enjoy Elite Dangerous:

- Expect EvE Online
- Expect a standard MMO experience
- Expect a single player RPG story
- Expect everything now
- Expect to be special in a universe where you mean nothing
- Expect to be safe from pvp in Open mode

There are other guidelines that could be added I'm sure, but put it this way - if you loved Frontier/ Frontier First Encounters, you'll like this. After 500 hours I've more than got my money's worth, even if I uninstall tomorrow. 

Are there flaws? Of course. Frontier are a small developer, and things take time. Some mechanics need a bit more depth, but in general you'll get a varied, truly beautiful galaxy, superb atmosphere, great flight model, and complete freedom. 

It's the best space sim available at the moment, in my view at least.

Edit: I would suggest that anyone who wants to get Elite Dangerous, but isn't in a hurry to buy it, to wait for the expansion Horizons. The expansion will cost 40 Euros, but come with the full elite dangeorus game + the expansion Horizons. The regular game will only unlock when the expansion is released, so no point in preordering (unless you already have elite dangerous and want the 10 Euro discount off horizon).

I like it, I'm leaving a positive review, but with a lot of caveats since this type of gameplay is definitely a niche taste.

Welcome to the literal entirety of the Milky Way galaxy. The community has successfully explored about 0.06% of the simulated galaxy since FDev's servers somehow have enough server space to simulate potentially 100 billion stars in the galaxy and travelling more than, say, a couple dozen thousand lightyears away from Earth happens to take an obnoxiously long time (though some players are crazy enough that they've done it). This game simulates distance incredibly well. Outer space is huge. ridiculously huge. There is no fast travel system; your spaceship that travels several times faster than the speed of light *is* your fast travel system. It just so happens that outer space is so utterly huge that it can still take many hours of real-world time investment to get anywhere--even at several times the speed of light--depending on how far you're trying to go: A "short" jump that would take 20 years at the speed of light from one solar system to the next can be done instantly with plenty of ships. A longer journey of 500 lightyears can take a whole afternoon (or instantly with very specialized ships and environmental circumstances giving you a boost), Travelling 5000 lightyears to sell wine at a remote billionaire's getaway resort in space can take the better part of an entire day of real-world time. Travelling to 20,000 light years to the Coloneia system -- generally accepted by the community as the furthest reach of populated space -- can take a couple weeks depending on what ship you're flying. Going 60,000 light years(!!) to Beagle Point can take the better part of a real-world month (at least so I'm told). Space is a pretty big place.

That's my first caveat: a LOT of your time in this game will be spent travelling, watching the "30,000 light seconds to next destination" indicator slowly tick down while your spaceship approaches it at a velocity that actually should just be straight-up fucking impossible within the known laws of physics. The game makes this process surprisingly difficult to get tired of: every spaceship's engine makes a different humming noise as it charges up, interiors are lovingly decorated and covered in sci-fi glowing lights. But suffice to say this is not a game where you can sit down and squeeze in a quick 15 minute session before work or school. You can't quite walk away from the computer while you're travelling either, because sometimes your ship's autopilot messes up and overshoots your target by a few thousand lightseconds or pirates will intercept you mid-travel trying to steal whatever you're carrying (or, if you're going through a system at war, the paranoid local authorities will casually pull you over for a spot check to make sure you're not fighting for 'the other guys').

Beyond that, gameplay really boils down to a few different tasks: combat, mining, exploring, trading. If you're like me, then combat is the only thing that actually feels exciting while the rest is just filler, but I would say the combat definitely feels great (albeit a little unvaried).
Transportation is basically a cozy mode, or there to let you do something productive while you're learning the game's complicated flying mechanics but otherwise gets tedious quickly. Exploration is a bit of the same but with a caveat: you make a ton of money by being the first player to discover new systems. This sounds like something that has a limited time utility but, again, after a full decade the playerbase has successfully explored about 0.06% of the simulated Milky Way galaxy and I have a feeling that we have better chances of discovering actual real-world insterstellar space travel before Elite Dangerous' simulated map of the Milky Way galaxy runs out of unexplored systems. The very first player to arrive in a star system, to map a new planet, to set foot on a world, gets their username PERMANENTLY slapped onto each and every planet they discover forever for all players who come after you to let them know that YOU. WERE. FIRST. Not as exciting as combat to me, but I know some players go absolutely nuts over exploration so that might be your thing if it's not mine.
Mining is an odd beast; it goes from very simple to ridiculously complicated and my current experience of it is that I literally made more money shooting down the NPC pirates who kept trying to steal my minerals than I got from actually selling the minerals themselves. It's the sort of thing where you need to look at guides and get advice from experienced players because it's more complicated than what the developers can bother explaining in-game. I think it should speak to the complexity of the game that I'm only just starting to learn mining now after 500 hours mostly focused on combat.

Oh, and there's xeno hunting too. There's currently a single hostile alien species known as the "Thargoids" who sometimes cause trouble, and you can deliberately go after them or ignore them as you wish. Again, 500 hours and I haven't even spotted my first Thargoid, let alone joined a Thargoid hunt.

The game labels itself as an MMO which is technically correct, but maybe not what most people expect when they hear that. There are discord communities where you can deliberately link up with other players and a "powerplay" system where you can cooperatively join a long-term team and work to spread your team's colour across the galaxy similar to Helldivers 2's territory system. That said, there's about 4000 concurrent players for a galaxy that's roughly to-scale of hundreds of billions of stars so it is incredibly rare to actually run into another player unless you're looking for them--and chances are if you run into another player in Open mode, you'll either ignore each other "like two ships in the night" as the saying goes, or the other guy is gonna try to randomly kill you for their own amusement. There is a solo option and I heartily endorse it until you've decided to join a Powerplay team and have an actual reason to interact with other players aside from being chased down by gankers. Aside from that, most of the galaxy is 'player-built'. Most of the space stations and planetary settlements you take resupply and take missions from are actual player-placed assets through the game's tedious but permanent colonization system. Like all MMOs, there's a microtransaction system, but you can earn ARX (the game's special premium currency) at a rate of 400 per week so it's not a permanent wall between haves-and-have-nots. At the time of this review, I can safely say that this feels like a game where it's safe to get invested in the long run since the monetization system doesn't feel like it's exclusively built to punish players who don't cough up more real-world money, which is honestly more than I can say for some bad purchases I've made in the past like the Company of Heroes franchise or even certain singleplayer games with hyper-aggressive DLC cycles (Paradox games, Creative Assembly games).

 Again, I think the big hangup some players have is once the 'honeymoon' phase wears off, some of the gameplay loops feel surprisingly same-y once you get the hang of it--but I think that applies to literally any game out there. Considering I managed to get this game for less than the price of a sandwich on a holiday sale, I'd say 500 hours is an excellent return on my money spent.

What's the least grindy way of getting materials for progression? Of course, that would be going to one specific location, and then logging in and out repeatedly for hours and recollecting the materials that respawn with 0 threat. Thought you would have any incentive to explore the "1:1 scale" replica of the entire galaxy, and hunt materials down yourself? Nope, unless you prefer dedicating literal weeks to only that, and not even coming close to what you would get from a few hours of just relogging. I'm not exaggerating. This is actually how shittily designed the game is. Oh, and there's a material limit too in your inventory, so you'll always have to do this again :)

How to earn credits to buy things? You can mine asteroids which is going to be over 50x more efficient than all the other activities, is the easiest, and there is zero threat of losing anything. Literally every time you enter a mining hotspot, there will be 1 pirate A.I. that scans you for cargo (which you have none of since you just got there), and then never interacts with you again. You can then mine all you want with no threat. If you log out and log back in, the game respawns the pirate near you though, and it will scan you and attack you unless you drop some cargo. There is no literally no variance at all to this.

Even with mining's stupid payouts, you still need to grind for hours and hours to outfit a ship, and that's not even including the material grind you'll have to do after to upgrade it. If you wanted to play the game leisurely doing whatever you wanted, it would take you actual weeks to make any amount of progression. And then after spending all this time trying to progress, you realize the game has zero fun or rewarding gameplay loops.
