[h1] What it takes to enjoy this game: [/h1]

[list]
[*] [b] Must be enthusiastic about space, space travel and sci-fi.[/b]

No "ifs", "ands" or "buts". If you don't like space, this game isn't for you.

[*] [b] Must enjoy or be intresested in simulation type games.[/b]

Understand that this is a simulation game at heart. If you are familiar with games like Eurotruck Simulator, then you have an idea of what I mean. There is a lot more gameplay than Eurotruck Simulator, but most of the appeal in this game comes from the feeling of commandeering your own ship.

[*] [b] Must be comfortable with completely open-ended gameplay.[/b]

If you prefer games with a solid clear objective, you may have a hard time coping with Elite Dangerous. There's nobody to tell you what to do but yourself. The deepest you can go in this game will only be as deep as you will dig. I know that sounds cliche, but that's what Elite is; it's your experience.

[*] [b] Must be able to tolerate a steep learning-curve.[/b]

Save for a few tutorial missions that teach you the basic controls and mechanics, most, if not all, of the skills you will acquire to play Elite Dangerous will be either by hours of Youtube explanations or just plain experience. If you haven't played many games that involve controlling a vehicle in fully 3D space, you might struggle for the first 50 hours of the game. Everything comes with practice. Some call that a "feature" and like games that don't hold your hand. If you you're one of those people this game might be for you. If not, that's okay too. Some very good games have very good tutorial systems, but this one isn't one of them.

[*] [b] Must be comfortable with "communities".[/b]

If you don't want to be associated with anybody outside a 10 kilometer radius of you, that's fine, but it may lead to some very bland experiences in Elite Dangerous. A lot of the depth comes from the active community who come together to make something special; whether it be an exploration expedition, a recent unkown discovery, or some stupid bullshit about a kid wizard. If you don't like people, there's always solo play, but that is cutting you out of an entire part of this game.[/list]

All in all, I hope this clears stuff up. If you don't think you'll like it, it's no problem. Elite is not like your average game.

Elite Dangerous is *not* a game. Do not buy it expected a smooth, easy to pick up experience. Elite is a Sim game with a gameplay loop. It's not about the combat, it's not about the mining, or the trading, or even the exploring. All of those are things you do in Elite, but Elite Dangerous - the game itself - is about the *experience* of flying a hyper-realistic ship in an obtusely realistic galaxy. It's frustrating, annoying, unintuitive, impactful, gritty, and the most fun flying in the entire genre. If you don't want a frustratingly precise minefield as your core gameplay loop, Elite's Probably not the game for you.

Elite is a game meant to be lived in, not merely played. The gameplay loops involve doing research on how it works, either in the ingame codex, or through third party tools. For many, that's a deal breaker and if that's you, Elite's probably not the game for you.

It's grindy. Elite's experience system *is* the credit system. Credit sinks are few, small, and far between for much of lifetime. What money you make, you only really lose when you mess up. As a result, you are constantly struggling to find the most efficient method of acquiring more and more wealth. And you always will be. If you're not the kind of player who enjoys the slow progression of accumulating wealth and power, Elite's probably not the game for you.

The story isn't about you. The *game* isn't about you. You are a citizen of this galaxy. One of millions and you just need to get used to that. The game recently finished a nearly three year war against an apocalyptic galactic threat. There were no heroes to laude, no storyline to play. Only events, won as a community. A story decided not by any individual player, but by the aggregate action of the entire playerbase. If you're looking for a game where you're the big damn hero? Elite's probably not the game for you.

If you're still here, you might be like me. You might want to buy peripherals like a Hands on Throttle and Stick. You might already own a VR headset. If you weren't any of the players that this game *wasn't* for... maybe this game *is* for you.

Let me preface this review by stating a fact: 

Elite: Dangerous is not a game for everyone. It is not a game with clear-cut storylines with questgivers and traditional questing frameworks. It is not a game with main characters and readily identifiable villains. It is a simple game with room for exactly as much complexity as you desire. 

Elite: Dangerous plops you down in a station, hands you the ignition card to a puny starship - a Sidewinder - and then points at the stars. "These belong to you," Elite says, "Go out and take them." 

And take them you shall. You can hunt bounties. You can take missions to assassinate pirate lords and military figureheads. You can smuggle drugs and weapons. You can haul relief supplies to famine and plague-stricken colonies. You can take to the far corners of the galaxy and spend months on long-haul expeditions scanning stars, moons, black holes, and myriad other anomalies and oddities across the void. You can operate outside the law, stalking freighters and committing heinous acts of terrorism and piracy, or you can operate a tramp freighter and chase profits across trading routes. You can throw out your cargo holds and replace them with passenger cabins, and taxi the rich and the destitute alike across the desolate sky. In the most recent updates, you can take the sword to the Xenos scum and drive them back from human space. 

Explorer, mercenary, pirate, smuggler, trader, xenos-hunter: these are but a few of the roles you can immerse yourself in, and nothing and no-one can stop you from switching between them. 

Perhaps you'll spend your gameplay floating around LHS 3447 in a barely-upgraded Cobra III, scratching out a living through odd jobs and whatever work seems most entertaining to you. There's nothing wrong with that. Or perhaps you'll spend your gameplay chasing after the biggest ships in the game, relentlessly pursuing ranking with the galaxy's superpowers and its shadowy engineers, earning and spending hundreds of millions to assemble for yourself the finest warship the galaxy has ever seen. Or maybe, just maybe, you'll be somewhere in the middle, content to carve your name into the galaxy with the heavy guns of a modestly-upgraded Python. 

Whatever you do, remember that Elite is a game about freedom. You have the freedom to choose. The factions you align yourself with, the stars you visit, the missions you take, the ships you fly, and the weapons you use - these are all choices you can make freely.  

This ultimate freedom is a weakness, of course, and it will leave some pilots wandering helpless and lost. That's okay. Elite is not an easy game, but it is a rewarding one. If you choose to join us among the stars, I ask only that you be patient. Rome was not built in a day, nor will you find yourself at the helm of an Anaconda in a week. There's greatness to be found in Elite - you just have to leave the station to find it.

It all started somewhere around autumn 2020 when Elite Dangerous was free on Epic Games. I picked it up with zero expectations. Just another free game to try, maybe spend a few evenings on and forget about. Instead, I’ve been stuck here ever since.

At the beginning I had no idea what I was doing. Docking felt like a boss fight, every jump felt risky, and making a few thousand credits actually felt like progress. It was slow, confusing, and honestly kind of clunky. But something about it kept pulling me back in. Not in an addictive “one more match” way, but more like a quiet curiosity. I wanted to understand it.

And that’s how it starts with Elite Dangerous. You don’t get hooked instantly. It grows on you.

You learn how to fly. Then how to survive. Then how to optimize. At some point you stop thinking about controls and start thinking in routes, systems, distances. The galaxy stops being overwhelming and starts becoming… familiar.

From there it just escalates.

I’ve done pretty much everything this game has to offer. Trading, exploration, combat, exobiology, engineering, long-haul travel. I didn’t specialize early on, I just kept going deeper into whatever felt interesting at the time. Eventually that turns into something else entirely. You stop playing “activities” and start setting your own goals. Fought global thargoid war, killed titan thargoids, made the absurd amount of money from that and i want more. 

That’s where most of my time went.

Long-term projects. The kind that sound cool at the start and then slowly turn into a grind. You tell yourself it’s worth it. Halfway through you’re not so sure anymore. But you keep going anyway because stopping feels worse than finishing.

I had moments where I was completely burned out. Logging in felt more like obligation than fun. The game has a way of doing that if you let it. It doesn’t always respect your time, and it definitely doesn’t try to keep you entertained every second.

And yet I kept coming back.

Part of it is just how the game feels. Flying a ship in Elite still hits different even after thousands of hours. The sound design, the scale, the way space actually feels empty instead of artificially busy. You can spend hours doing almost nothing and somehow it still works. There’s a kind of atmosphere here that other games try to replicate but never quite get right.

But it’s not all good.

Odyssey release was rough. Probably the roughest period this game has ever had. Performance issues, bugs, design choices that made you question what they were even going for. It felt unfinished, and for a lot of people that was the breaking point.

I didn’t quit, but I won’t pretend it didn’t affect the experience. That was one of those moments where you really see both sides of this game. The potential and the frustration at the same time.

Then there was the Thargoid war.

That’s one of the things Elite actually did right. A large-scale conflict that players could take part in. Not just background lore, but something you could actively engage with. I fought in it, took part in Titan kills, watched systems fall and get pushed back. It wasn’t perfect, but it felt like being part of something bigger than just your own progress.

Moments like that remind you why you stuck around.

Somewhere along the way I also started doing stuff outside the game. Made a video ranking all ships with memes, because after this many hours you either go insane or start creating things out of it.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-VDRUTXFwf8

And at some point I realized I actually have a full commander history written down:

https://inara.cz/elite/cmdr-biography/319802/

Looking at that now is kind of surreal. You don’t notice the time passing while you’re playing. It just accumulates. Then suddenly you’re sitting on thousands of hours and a whole timeline of things you’ve done.

So yeah, is Elite Dangerous a good game?

That depends on what you expect.

If you want something fast, rewarding, constantly exciting, this probably isn’t it. The game is slow. It’s repetitive. It will waste your time if you’re not careful. There are systems that feel outdated and mechanics that could have been improved years ago.

But if you’re the kind of person who enjoys long-term progression, setting your own goals, and just existing in a massive world without being rushed… then it’s something special.

This isn’t a game you “finish”.

It’s a game you stay in for a while.

Sometimes you leave for weeks or months. Then you come back, do a few jumps, hear the engines again, and it just clicks like it always did.

I started this thinking I’d play for a few hours because it was free.

6.5k hours later, I’m writing a review on a different platform after transferring my account, still coming back to it from time to time.

That probably says more than anything else I could write here.

[b]Recommended.[/b]

But only if you understand what you’re signing up for.

If you've always wanted to explore the stars yourself.
If you love customization, optimization, and fine-tuning your spaceship of choice for the task at hand.
If you're a fan of absolutely superb sound design.

What to say about Elite...

Firstly, the game itself is incredible, in many ways.

It's incredibly beautiful. Any screenshot of some of the most mundane stuff is absolutely amazing. The engine, though somewhat dated, is extremely complex, going down into detail to such things as how planetary atmosphere compositions scatter and bend light into different wavelengths, or how star systems that were randomly generated at the start of the game were made as realistically as we know. It helps that Frontier Developments actually enlisted the help of astrophysicists and the like to help design the engine; many members of that team are actually memorialized in the game one way or the other.

Elite is incredibly massive. The game has been around since 2014 (2013 if you want to be technical). A decade later, and certainly not for lack of trying, less than a percent of the galaxy has been mapped. It is just so incredibly large, so diverse, that it may take the entire community many, many lifetimes, no exaggeration, to map even a full percent. The scale is, pun intended, truly astronomical, and goes a long way to showing you just how small we are.

Elite is incredibly rich; the lore itself dates back to the original game from 1984, and reading the codex, you can even see the references about it all. The galaxy is very much alive, especially now that Frontier has gotten their heads back on it seems (more on that later), with events constantly happening and being driven by the playerbase. This is the community's story as a whole, for sure, but there's a whole few thousand years of history from before Elite:Dangerous came into being, so to speak, starting all the way from Yuri Gagarin launching to space. It's scattered across the sect of human-colonized space colloquially called the 'bubble' in the forms of data beacons, abandoned megaships, and more, all with their own story behind them.

Elite is, however, incredibly, INCREDIBLY grindy. It has been made much easier with recent updates, but those updates were too long in coming and certainly saw a large portion of potential players and seasoned commanders leaving before they happened. Money isn't the grind, it's the materials required to upgrade your ship's modules, weapons, and more to be 'the best' at your chosen profession, be it bounty hunting, exploring, fighting for one of the galactic superpowers, fighting the alien invaders and defending humanity on what was, until recently, a losing war, or more. Again, made much easier now, but even if it was enough, it was still too late.

Elite is incredibly frustrating. I say this as someone who experienced it personally; starting as a new player, expect to be ganked by seasoned veterans who have nothing better than to constantly kill fresh players because it's the only way they can level themselves up; anyone with half a brain would wipe them. Of course, in light of that, there are communities of players who dedicate themselves to hunting those same players down and clearing the way for those fresh players, and now you have solo play, where only you will be in your galaxy; you still share it with the rest of the playerbase, but you won't see them and they won't see you (NPCs can and will still try to take your cargo though, you aren't safe). Every now and then, a game bug will cause you to experience catastrophic damage to your ship, or a NPC pirate (or player) will interdict your cargo ship and kill you a few thousand kilometers (about 3 seconds' flight time) from your destination, but that's how it is. Brutal and frustrating. And you can't always rely on the security forces to help you out.

The biggest gripe with Elite isn't the game, but the company running it. Frontier Developments, for the last few years, chose to virtually abandon what can be described as their flagship title to pursue other genres of games, some of which worked, most of which flopped. While I'm all for companies trying new things and broadening their horizons, that firstly shouldn't be done at the cost of a very well-loved, money-making franchise, and secondly, if those new things fall flat, don't try to keep pumping them up, especially when the hole causing the leak still exists. At the start of this year (2024), Fdev had a little sit down with their folks, shareholders, etc etc, and figured out that maybe, instead of trying things that still aren't working for them, they should focus on the things that have been. Granted, that introduced some new monetization into the game, but it isn't even close to pay-to-win, or even pay-to-progress-faster...maybe along the lines of pay-to-skip-a-bit-of-that-grind-I-mentioned-earlier. And of course, there's skins for your ships, space suits, and surface vehicles. Many customization for many things, but the currency can be earned, 400 ARX (the premium currency) every week, simply playing the game. No missions to do, just play the game your way, and you'll earn it. And if you're adverse to spending any money but want some sort of customization? Every now and then, for holidays, community events, etc, you can earn some stuff by completing a set of missions that might have you go on a bit of a goose chase, or complete 'x' objective in concert with the rest of the playerbase to unlock new tech with bonus skins for certain contribution tiers. Credit where credit is due, Fdev do seem to be trying, but myself and many other long-time commanders are remaining wary.

Elite is certainly a game worth buying if you have time, and a lot of it. Expect to get addicted, if you enjoy space and science fiction, but that ebbs and flows. Find your niche in the game, and learn to love it, but don't be afraid to try out new things too. And there's always a group of players who can and will help you out, as long as you find the right ones.

I discovered this "game" in December 2017, and have racked up well over 1500 hours as of May 2018. I've barely touched anything else in my fairly extensive game library since then, and I feel it's for good reason. This isn't so much a "game" as it is a "toy", and what I mean by that is that there is very little structure, and a lot of room for the user to carve their own experience out of it.

This probably explains any negative reviews that you see here. If you go into this deal thinking that your hand is going to be held, and that your character is the presumed savior/chosen one of the galaxy, you are going to have a bad time. This is a cold, merciless simulator, not a videogame.

Everything from piloting your ship to trading between stations requires learning, and a lot of trial and error. You will fail a lot at first. You will curse at the controls when you try to land your ship, and you may even splatter yourself on a star if you don't pay attention to your throttle. Casual gamers coming from an MMO like World of Warcraft might not be appreciative of this learning curve.

For me, however, it has been like a second life. Every night when the wife and kids go to sleep, I strap on the Oculus, plug in the HOTAS, and live my very own science-fiction epic that I have completely forged on my own. I have also made friends all around the world who share the same enthusiasm and spirit of adventure.

However, even as a solo experience, there is so much to see and do in this game that it is literally impossible to get bored. A lot of my own enthusiasm probably comes from the fact that I am in my mid-40s, and have waited since I was about eight years old for a gaming experience like this one.

Some other positive points on Elite:Dangerous

The graphics are absolutely stunning, and some sights that I have seen throughout the Milky Way have been literally breathtaking.

The experience can either be white knuckle and adrenaline fueled gameplay like in combat, or it could be a chilled out affair where you listen to music or podcasts while mining asteroids. It's entirely up to you.

There are third-party applications like VoiceAttack and the HCS Voice Packs which make the experience even more immersive than it already is.

The galaxy that is opened up to you is your own, not some fictional or fantastical realm. NASA just discovered a new exo planet? Fly out and take a look at it for yourself!

Frontier Developments has stayed with their commitment to constantly improve and add more content to the game.

[b]I have a love hate relationship with Elite Dangerous[/b].....I WANT to recommend Elite Dangerous...and I was going to but I cant.

Elite Dangerous is a space sim. Its very science fiction but plausible and obeys its own rules for the most part. You are just another dude in the galaxy. Start out in your little sidewinder and then once your done the very basic tutorials the galaxy is free and open to you. 

Elite does a fantastic job of making you feel small. It still gives me the willies jumping to a pulsar. The galaxy is one to one with the milky way and it is big enough that you can go get lost somewhere no one will ever find you. There is a lot of different activities in the sandbox to get stuck into as well. Combat, trade, and exploration are all represented in the galaxy and I will say you CAN have a lot of fun with the game. But....

There is so much standing in the way of that fun. Constant reminders that the game could be better.

As a new player the first thing you are likely to encounter as a frustrating hurdle is the controls. Elite Dangerous has enough keybinds to compete with Arma. Now to be fair IT IS a simulator so that comes with the territory. After some time you will eventually learn or rebind all your necessary controls and the menus stay consistent and mostly intuitive. That is where that ends though....

Elite Dangerous' biggest crime is that in order to understand just about anything you have to open up a guide in the background....the tutorials are notoriously bad in Elite and this isn't something I can forgive. It is so unintuitive at times it borders on being esoteric and this would be OK if the game had deep complexly interwoven systems.....but after a while you start to realise that what your doing when you first try an activity and what your doing 100 hours later is the exact same thing. 

Elite has a lot of things to try sure but they all are surface level. Engineering teases you with the potential to adding some depth to things but all it does is make you more efficient at the same activities you were already doing. The time and effort investment for engineering is pretty large too which brings me to another problem of Elite.

The Grind. I am not apposed to it. I have played games that are worse than elite for grind but those games had more depth to their various activities......I can't help but feel Elite Dangerous uses grind to cover up the fact that there is little in the way of content in the game. Maybe to play on the sunk cost fallacy? I don't know.

My biggest frustration with Elite? The absolutely ridiculous justice system in game. Get in the way of a docking pad that you are not assigned for a little too long you get a fine. Sure seems reasonable. Except then the faction you have that fine with refuses to service your ship until you pay the fine. This wouldn't be so bad if it wasn't SO.....DAMN.....EASY.....to get fines in the game. This is if your lucky too. Sometimes when you get certain fines you get a bounty....those you can't pay off at the station and have to do so somewhere else OR....turn yourself in....

I tell you what, it sure is fantastic turning myself in for a 900 credit bounty which teleports you to a prison ship.....cool rollplay sure. But then your ship is impounded.....then that 900 credit fine that you STILL HAVE TO PAY even though you went to jail turns into 300'900 credit fine because your ship gets impounded....

Apparently the simulator part of elite dangerous is the dystopian bureaucracy..... 

I love Elite Dangerous. 
But...
I hate Elite Dangerous.

[b]I can't recommend people play elite dangerous. But I also won't say you shouldn't....[/b]
All I can do is be honest with what I have experienced and yall can make your choice.

I'm not far away from giving this game a positive review. I've certainly played enough hours.  
The foundations of the game's ships are some of the best that space sims have to offer. The ships feel and sound incredible.

But, as common as the sentiment might be, I feel it's important to talk about the game's depth, because I don't really see this particular perspective discussed enough.  
At a certain point, the basic novelty wears off and you see the underlying system more clearly. 
Pretty much everything loops back into the same mission board cycle and monetary/rank based ship progression.  
Unlocking/fitting out later ships of course allows you to tackle more difficult missions and targets, but... That's really it. Nothing else really changes alongside you.  

The depth, here, isn't so much about a lack of content. It's about a lack of meaningful context. What's missing is a sense of purpose, of belonging, of consequence, recognition.  

The factions are the best example I have of this.  
You can  join the Federation or Empire and work your way up their ranks - but nothing meaningful about the game changes at any point. 
You can unlock faction-specific ships, but your relationship to the faction feels fundamentally the same as not being associated to that faction at all. It's the same recycled missions as before, just with a faction symbol tied to it, and nothing of real consequence or progress other than a number increasing over time. 

I want joining a faction to actually feel like joining a faction. I want to defend their territory, support their logistics, participate in offensives, respond to strategic threats and feel like I occupy a real role within a faction or military, like my rank means something and carries duty, responsibility. 
Not necessarily through scripted linear content; there's no need to scrap the mission board foundation. But what I feel is missing is systems that make the factions and wider systems react to who you are and how you're committing yourself. 
  
And honestly, I don't think Elite is that far away from having a basic, achievable version of that kind of immersion that could be expanded on over time.
 
I've heard people respond these kinds of criticims by saying "It's a sandbox" or something to the effect of "You make your own goals" but I find this to be dismissive, as it neglects to see how we can have both.
The game already has an excellent foundation. What's missing, for me, is the substance inside the sandwich.

[h1]Introduction[/h1]
At the time of writing this I got 8 hours clocked + 5 hours spent in the "unofficial" combat demo the day before steam release. Thus I will not go into the "end game", but rather describe the initial experience. I'll update the review once I reach a 100 hours played.

[b]This game is hardcore, do not expect it to hold your hand![/b] Really, that's the most important thing to state, and it is the #1 point that the negative reviews list here. However, I don't think it is a negative point. It's an intentional part of the game, and you either like it or you do not. Expect to spend your first hours of playing by going through the combat and travel tutorials and really suck at it. Then spend the rest of your day on constantly looking up youtube videos and articles on the Elite: Dangerous wiki each time you want to try something new. It is part of the charm, and if you push through it you will truly enjoy it. Once you're past this and you managed to figure out how to make some money (tip: go bounty hunting near Nav points!), you'll notice the beauty of this game.

A tip is to find the unofficial combat demo, and try for yourself whether you like how the ship control feels or not. Ask around on [url=reddit.com/r/elitedangerous]reddit.com/r/elitedangerous[/url]. You can ask any other question about the game there too! Also take the first few hours tweaking the controls. With mouse/kb: setting the Mouse X-axis to yaw instead of roll (and mapping A/D to roll left/roll right) makes a huge difference. 


[h1]THE GOOD[/h1]
[list]
[*] There are many ways to make money, and it's up to you which ones you want to do. You can have multiple ships, so you can switch up playstyles. The big money is in trading. Not your thing? Go hunt the other traders as you become a pirate! Want to be more "legal"? Become a bounty hunter and hunt the pirates! Want to explore the literally billions of star systems (most of which haven't been visited by players yet)? Grab a better jump drive and exploration scanner, and earn cash by mapping unexplored systems as a space explorer!

[*] The game is visually stunning! Not just in its graphics, but also in the sheer scale of things; travelling from one end of the galaxy to the other might take months.

[*] Controlling your space ship [i]feels[/i] good. There are so many little options, and even a thing as docking is more than just pushing a button. Yes, docking to a space ship can actually be one of the most lethal things you'll be doing.
[/list]


[h1]THE BAD[/h1]
[list]
[*] Player interaction is minimal. Despite being a multiplayer game, it is actually hard to find other players, I expected it to be more like freelancer where it is easy to contact any player within your system or even further out (without being friends). Ultimately this game is mainly a solo PvE experience unless you find friends to play with. You can run some of the more popular trade routes for a couple hours and not encounter more than 2 or 3 other players.

[*] IF you find other players, you might not actually like it. Obviously there are players who shoot everyone on sight (even camping the new player systems), or just had the same plan as you for making money by killing NPC criminals in the same area, which makes you compete for kills (only the last hit on an enemy grants the reward). Others play pirate, but so far the player pirates I have encountered are kind people playing their role, so that actually does not bother as much.

[*] The game feels shallow. It is a mile wide and an inch deep, as people say. There are big updates coming to the game though, so it'll gradually get better. It would be great if a thing like the EVE corporations (or guilds/clans) would be more incorporated into the game. Let the players craft the story. Right now, the most profit can be gained from interacting with NPCs (pirating, bounty hunting, trading), which make the multiplayer aspect a bit sad.
[/list]

EDIT 6/4/'15: As some of you have pointed out, the docking issues with too many players trying to dock at the same time might just be temporary, and are mainly a thing at the small stations in the new player systems. It is still a nuisance though, but I agree that the problem kind of solves itself after you're further out.

Phenomenal experience. Steep learning curve (don't trust reviews that couldn't make it past the initial hump). Incredibly granular. And, most of all, GORGEOUS.

Sound design is on an entirely different level. The entire game continually blows my mind with its depth, scale, and attention to detail.

I'm a miner, explorer, and bounty hunter. I fight for freedom. I fight for peace.

Literally the only complaint I have with the game is that it requires 3rd party sites to get the most out of it. If you choose to pick up Elite, then bookmarkthe following sites: inara.cz, eddb.io, coriolis.io, and roguey.co.uk —these will save you SO much time and confusion.

I also recommend watching some starter guides on YouTube. This is an oldschool game that isn't about to hold your hand and sugar coat the universe for you. It's gonna drop you in the middle of a random system and let you figure it out from there.

Either you like that (like me), or you don't. That doesn't make the game bad, but it does separate the wheat from the chaff right off the bat. People keep saying they want difficult oldschool-style games, and then they get this and QQ about how it's too hard to figure out (see 80% of the negative reviews). If you crave that classic game that challenges you to use your brain, then you're going to love Elite. If you're looking for an arcade-like space fighter... yeah, might wanna move along to the next thing.

I started playing this game about a month ago.  I downloaded EVE because I had seen several posts online claiming you could play it in some sort of PvE-only mode.  As an older gamer (ok, I'm 31, but still) I do not play PvP any more.  I've gotten sick of the drama and the cheating and the spawn camping and just wanted to fly around a space ship and shoot enemies who don't insult my mother whenever I hit them.  Sadly, I discovered that the handful of people claiming you could play EVE in a PvE-only mode were wrong, and I went looking for an alternative.

That's when I found Elite Dangerous.  The reason I'm writing this review is to highlight a single, MASSIVE feature that hasn't gotten anywhere near the attention it deserves in other reviews: Solo and Private Group Modes.  With these, you can play the game - the entire game, minus other players - in peace, alone or with up to 3 friends.  No griefing, no spawn camping, no BS human shenanigans.  You'll still get interdicted by NPCs and such, but when you do, they'll do it once, and if you successfully evade the interdiction, they leave you alone and you can go on your merry way.  (Plus with certain Assassination missions, this saves you investing in a FSD Interdictor yourself, instead you can just submit to the NPC's interdiction.)

What makes this even better is that it's all linked.  Anything you do in Solo Mode transfers over to Open Mode (wide open PvP enabled with other players, etc.)  Thus, even if you like PvP, you can still play in Solo Mode until you get your bearings and get a good, well-equipped ship (and save enough extra money for insurance.  DON'T FLY WITHOUT YOUR REBUY!) and then switch to Open Mode and have far less trouble getting owned.  Personally, I won't ever be playing Open Mode, but Private Group mode will be a lot of fun when I get a couple of my friends on, and and knowing that everything I've done in Solo Mode will transfer over is just wonderful.

There's all manner of other fun, cool stuff I could go on and on about, but every other reviewer has already done that.  I just wanted to highlight this specific feature because I've not seen it in any of the other competing games.

What a weird game.

More so than any other game I've played, I wish I could leave a "I have no idea if I enjoyed this" rating. 

Elite has the single best space flight model I've personally ever encountered. That's the strength of the game. Frankly, I think the game started out as "let's develop a really great flight model" and, once the devs had that figured out, they decided to embed it into a one-to-one scale model of the Milky Way with trading, fighting, mining, planetary exploration and more as a side project.

I think I played Elite in a much different way than most. I never once played in open. I only ran missions or fought to amass enough credits to upgrade my ship. Instead I set out on a lonely journey across the stars in search of a little tendril of the Milky Way to call my own. For the first few hours, days, weeks it was pure wonder. Recklessly jumping into unknown systems with no repair, no rescue, no clue, just to see what was there. Black holes, neutron stars, binary systems, water worlds, and even the rare Earth-like: I couldn't get enough. There was something that always impressed me and struck equal parts of awe and fear into me. You'd be out flying aimlessly in a general direction and then spot something interesting in the distance. Perhaps it was just a particularly bright or colorful star. Perhaps it was an oddly organized cluster. Maybe you could just barely make out a wisp of a nebula. And so you'd set your course, and jump by jump, hour by hour, you'd start making your way towards it until its scale struck you with its grandiosity. The closest analogy I have is when you notice a mountain in the distance, drive toward it for five hours, and realize that the mountain has gotten no bigger. You begin to comprehend just how [i]large[/i] this thing actually is. I still don't like going into nebulae.

At some point, without having realized it, I had settled into a routine. Many people describe Elite as "grindy"; I see where they're coming from, but---in my experience---I have to disagree. I didn't play Elite because I felt like I [i]had to[/i], playing Elite was just what I [i]did[/i]. I'd probe the stars, jumping and scanning, for a few hours after work while listening to music, podcasts, movies, and shows. It became a nightly ritual, somewhere between ennui and content. I had never lost that sense of awe, that sense of scale, and it managed to scratch that itch for metrizable progress. You could see [i]exactly[/i] how many hundreds of light-years you jumped that evening, or how many planets you had scanned. One of my major projects was to jump clear across the galaxy and back; playing for a handful of hours most nights, it ended up taking me two or three weeks in real time. There are very, very few games that not only have goals on this scale but also let you [i]create your own goals[/i] on this scale.

Scale and grandiosity are not without their failures. You can only jump so far before you start noticing the veneer begin to peel. There are only a few dozen (hundred?) models for any given planet or star, there are only so many visual and auditory effects, and---most tragically of all---there are only so many ships to fly. Elite stopped being a source of inspiration and started being a task where I chronicled which permutation of the same few ingredients I happened to run into that night (kind of like Taco Bell). 

That is not to say I stopped playing. I went back to the bubble to be with my fellow man (and, in some cases, to blast that fellow man into sweet nonexistence for having the gall to scan a fully strapped 'vette for loot). I mined and grinded. I tried my hand at space trucking. I squished some (small) bugs. I spent hours min-maxing ship builds for all different purposes. But no matter what I did, I could still feel the black calling for me. The void had lost its sparkling luster, though, and I had seen all that I could see. 

Or so I thought. I set out many months ago for one final mission. I wanted to find somewhere quiet, somewhere out in the far reaches of space to put my ships down for good. I wasn't playing Elite much anymore, if at all, but one last journey sounded fun for the first time in a while. It was only then, after hundreds of hours---most of which being spent [i]exploring[/i] and actually [i]looking for things[/i]---that I (accidentally) stumbled across my first stellar phenomena. For the first time in a long time I felt that sense of awe, that sense of trepidation. It wasn't enough to pull me back in, but it was a nice reminder of what made the game special to me in the first place (as well as a reminder of the scale of the game; I had explored tens of thousands of systems by this point, seen (almost) all of the assets the game had, and I was [i]still[/i] running into things I hadn't found before).

The sky box has always been my favorite part of the game, dynamically updating to give you a unique view depending on which system you were in. It means you can visually plot a course to something interesting in the sky, and see how far you'd already come or how far you still had to go. On an outer arm of the galaxy you can pick out isolated clusters of stars looking rimward, and hubward is the gentle glow of the galactic center occluded by massive sectors of interstellar dust. In the center it is a continuum of stars, each more brilliant than the last; even in the shadow of the furthest moon, there is no darkness. Nebulae float in the sky like drops of paint in water, suspended in time by their sheer size. Visiting one gives you vistas of incomparable color. 

There is one place---or, many, I suppose---that I find more special than any other: the edge. The further from the center you go, the thinner the star field grows, until, at the very edge, there are but tenuous systems, barely holding on to the galaxy by the thinnest gossamer gravity can provide. When you reach one of these system, you will finally get to behold it. Face your ship away from the system's star and fly out. Fly for ten minutes straight. Stop your ship, disable your power, and look. The black. Unlike reality, there is no sky box in Elite outside of the stars that exist in the Milky Way (and a few other features, like the Magellanic clouds). In reality, you'd be staring at a myriad of unknown galaxies, clusters, and lone stars. In Elite, there is nothing but the black. In many ways it is unnerving after being surrounded by unknown stars. In another, it is pure calm. There are no more systems to jump. There are no more moons to explore. There are no more "I've been in super cruise for seventeen minutes and there's nothing on my scanners ... I'll just run to the bathroom for thirty secon-annnnd I'm being interdicted." Elite doesn't have an endgame, but the black is mine. I've set my beloved DBX out, powered down, facing out into the void, somehow infinitesimal and gargantuan compared to what it now looks out upon.

With all of that said, I [i]STILL[/i] don't know if I would recommend the game. It's open ended with no real purpose. It's incredibly shallow outside of the flight model. Some of the mechanics are clearly half-baked, both in terms of designs and implementation. With Elite, I think too many people focus on what the game [i]isn't[/i] rather than what it [i]is[/i]. I think it's something really special. I just don't know if it will be special for you. I'd sum it up with this: if there is one game I could wipe my memory of, it'd be Elite so I could experience the magic of jumping to another system for the first time again. 

As a final aside: as an online only game, Elite's days are numbered. I sincerely hope FDev will release an end-of-life plan that will allow us---even if it's only single player---to play the game after they shut down the servers and end support. Even if I don't see myself playing Elite again, losing the game entirely would be a tragedy.

As many who play, I have always desired to embark into the great unknown of space.  Only I was born to early. From system permits to capitol ships to engineers, this sim requires dedication and rewards only those who have the intestinal fortitude to perservere through the dullness that space life can be. Jumping system to sytem, checking the local map and seeing the names of the CMDRs who came before you, planting there name forever on the planets you come across on your journey, seems redundant. I've got 140+ hours in Elite: Dangerous. From trading in an Adder, to running drugs and guns between systems in a Cobra, to that revelatory moment when I took my beloved Asp deep into the Pleiades and saw my first black hole up-close, there have been some fantastic moments in this game.

However, once you've smuggled enough weapons to fund the next 20 years of wars, and taken your ship tens of thousands of light years deep into the galactic core, you start to realize how empty this galaxy is. It's a beautiful galaxy, but a lifeless one. The thrill of seeing your first black hole, or stumbling on a new type of exotic star, or dropping out of supercruise to surf the debris rings around a Jovian, can't overcome the vast emptiness of Elite's galaxy.

The complaint that this game is lacking content comes up so often because it's irrefutably true. There are only two general designs for starbases. Every starbase in the game has the same exact sign, scuffed in the same exact places, in every docking port. 

Once you get beyond human space, you will never, ever be surprised by anything you find, you will never be in danger, and you will never encounter anything but planets, stars and astroid belts. There are no comet swarms, no dynamic phenomena, no stars going nova, This is a science fiction game, but there are no derelict starships, no long-abandoned starbases built by alien civilizations, no distant planets in far-flung corners of the galaxy with ruins suggestinig intelligent life, no Dyson spheres, no inscrutable megastructures, no ringworlds, no artilects or machine consciousnesses, no nanoswarms, no artifacts.

There's that famous J.B.S. Haldane quote that's often quoted in discussions about science fiction: "Not only is the universe stranger than we imagine, it is stranger than we can imagine."

But not Elite's universe. Elite's galaxy is a lonely, lifeless place where you will never be surprised by anything.

Regarding the content, as other reviewers have pointed out, this is essentially a late stage alpha/early beta that needs a lot more content to help flesh it out. But instead of acknowledging how light the game is on content, the developers are releasing new content as expansions, condescendingly calling those expansions "Early Access," and using a pricing scheme that inexplicably punishes players who already have the base game.

So we've got devs selling a beta (at best), charging full price for unfinished "expansions" and calling them "Early Access" expansions to make up for the fact that the content expansions are lacking in content. It's essentially pre-ordering DLC for a game that isn't even close to being finished.

And what do the expansions give us? The much-heralded Horizons gives us procedurally generated, airless rock worlds and buggies. That's it. If you were hoping for waterworlds, or atmospheric worlds with teeming jungles, or bizarre alien landscapes, you'll be sorely disappointed, because all you'll get is rock with a few random outposts thrown in for good measure.

What can I say about Elite that hasn't already been said by everyone else? 

It has it's flaws, there is no getting around that; 

* There is a steep learning curve, and outside of a basic flight tutorial the game makes zero effort to point you in any kind of real direction, explain the mechanics (there are a lot of them), tell you where/how to find literally -anything- in game, or how anything works. At all. 

* If you fly in Open (and you should absolutely fly in Open) there are elements of the community that are nothing short of toxic ass-hats that will kill you for fun. 

* The Dev's are often willfully deaf to the valid complaints of the player base (the BGS is broken).

* It's a grind. All of it. Engineers, then suit engineers, then farming enough materials to engineer your ships, then getting a Fleet Carrier, etc. It's a lot of work, and you'll be doing a lot of the same thing, over, and over, and over.

* Odyssey launched as a laughable mess; the FPS element was (and largely still is) shallow and sophomoric, the frame-rate was almost unplayable, and we didn't even get ship legs.


But it's worth every penny (yes, at full price), and more. 
Between Epic and Steam, I have well over 3,000 hours in Elite, and I've loved every minute of that time. 

The experience of launching yourself into a 1:1 representation of our galaxy and having the freedom to do whatever you want is priceless. 

I've spent days in asteroid belts mining raw metals and minerals, hauling them laboriously to the station with the best buy price, and building my credit balance.

I've fought pirates, rival factions and giant alien's in everything from the stock Sidewinder to fully engineered Anaconda's (the snake names are a theme, you get used to it). 

I've hauled hundreds of thousands of tons of cargo to build stations, ground installations and orbital platforms in systems I've colonized.

I've spent literal, real-time months out in the Black exploring, scanning strange flora, and seeing star systems, stellar phenomenon and planets no one has ever seen before (which gets your name attached to that system forever). 

The beauty of Elite (aside from the actual beauty, and let me tell you there are some breathtaking views to be seen) is that it is exactly what you make it. I’ve heard it said that Elite Dangerous has no soul.

But I’m here to tell you that it does. I know, because I found it.

At first I doubted it, too. I mean, sure, from the time I climbed into my starting Sidey, strapped the shoulder harnesses on and flew out of that first Coriolis, I’ll admit it; I was blown away by the visuals. And the sound, too. Isn’t everybody? It really was very magnificent. But where was the game? What was I supposed to do? It wasn’t obvious. Just the opposite in fact. Space was black as the bottom of a coal bucket and endlessly, impossibly huge. Where were all the amazing sci-fi staples, such as neon colored nebula that were so bright they lit the screen with their pretty colors? There were no quest markers to tell me where to go. No guideposts, no “attaboy!” taps on the shoulder every thirty seconds for having not died, or successfully left the airlock, or some other trivial activity.

My screen didn’t start magically popping with messages and tutorials and information about such and such quests that were suddenly available. I was left alone to figure out things, and what became apparent pretty quickly was that I wasn’t ever going to even make enough money to get to the next ship up, much less be the ruler of the universe at some near point in the future. I flew into the hotspots where a great deal of the game’s combat takes place, or so I gathered at the time. I engaged hostiles with my pitiful kpew kpew lasers in combat inspired more by a surrealistic take on WWI aerial combat than anything resembling hard science fiction; the Sideys engines roared and grumbled, and when I banked to come about to keep track of an enemy, it sounded and felt like the rivets in the floor panels were struggling to fly apart under the stress of the manoeuvre. Everything happened at point blank range.

Still no pop-ups telling me what to do.

I struggled with landing, and when in stations I visited various mission bulletin boards that held a bewildering array of missions that if I happened to be qualified to accept in the first place paid peanuts and were very unclear about how to accomplish, and most spoke of distances far greater than my starter ship could even reasonably be expected to jump.

I worked with the game, struggling to learn its mechanics and features, but felt little sense of progress. I had fun and felt like I got my money’s worth...but after the initial amazement over the game’s visuals and sound wore off, I slowly began to lose interest. I felt like after I visited one Resource Extraction Site I had seen them all. The same for the 2-4 station models. The “world” was vast, but lacked personality, a reason to explore its contours and borders.

It seemed like those who claimed the game had no soul were right after all...

And then on one cold, boring day in December, Horizons released and I decided to pick it up and give the game another chance. I landed on airless worlds that were as rugged as they were beautiful, deploying my SRV like a futuristic 4-wheeler and exploring everything, from mysterious downed satellites to rare and useful mineral deposits that could be used for crafting everything from ammo upgrades to jump boosts.

Suddenly, my interest was engaged and the story telling part of my brain kicked in; I was Han Solo, and my ship was my Millennium Falcon. I smuggled slaves, one step ahead of the law; I ran blockades, joined Power Play, learned how to survive unwanted PvP and began to define an identity within the game’s universe. For the first time I felt like even though I would never be the master of all I surveyed, the identity of my CMDR was enough. I joined a group of Intergalactic hippies and followed them for over two months to the very edge of the galaxy where we stood shoulder to shoulder as brothers and sisters and gazed into the abyss, the dark night between galaxies before us, the blazing golden band of the galaxy’s core running from horizon to horizon over our shoulders. Many of us had ships that were so beat up from the voyage out that there was little hope of making it home.

As I took a moment to contemplate the game, the scope and breadth of the galaxy I’d traversed for no better reason than to say I did it and to shake my fist in defiance at that strange, black alien sky, I finally realized that I had been wrong: Elite Dangerous does have a soul...but it is cold and austere, a chill wind that blows through your center when you’ve been pushed to the point where you feel you’re made of glass and will surely break. It will only reveal itself to you when the immensity of the game finally, crushingly sinks into your bones.

Oh yes, Elite does indeed have a soul, but it’s not for everybody. It is only for those who persevere, those who adapt, survive and prevail against all odds. For those of you who would shake your fists at the sky and shout the devil down from the arch of time, I salute you, for you too are Elite.

I feel inclined to leave a review as a new player who broke through the unfriendly first stages.

Like most of the recent reviews cropping up, when I first played Elite I hated it. I hated it so much, I uninstalled it in a fit of pure, white-hot rage with less than 2 hours of playtime.

None of it made sense. The game was very willing to let me make every mistake under the sun, after I spent an entire tutorial doing very little related to flying an actual ship. The game THEN let me outfit a ship in the worst possible way, unable to effectively jump to a small distance away to complete the single mission I had taken on.

"Who the f*** would enjoy this?"

But a friend with many hours challenged me... 'I'm surprised you just left it'. So I swallowed my frustration, re-installed and decided I would figure this shit out.

Elite is not a friendly game.
Elite is not a game that explains itself.
Elite -will- let you make mistakes. Some of those mistakes feel extremely unfair. A lot of these mistakes happen early on.
Elite is a game where gameplay is measured in hundreds of hours. Don't expect to be kitted out at a top level after 20-30 hours of investment.
The ARX store exists. There are microtransactions. Remember: this is a 10 year old game being sold at a fraction of its price. They sell things to help fund development. The new ships have doubled the monthly player count (over 2024) which is hard to complain about (and all the new ships are stunning). They are reasonably priced and will let you skip the grind. Love it or hate it, it's there.
Elite is a game about flying. That's the whole thing. You fly so you can get more stuff to get a better/cooler ship that you can... fly. That's it.

If you can get over those things above, and you enjoy a good gameplay loop in a sim... well, there ain't nothing else like it.

With an eye-tracker and a HOTAS, you will feel like you're really in your ship, blasting around asteroids and zipping through shipyards. The sound is sublime, the galaxy is beautiful (and terrifying), and the ship designs are fantastic (and even the ones that aren't will grow on you). You can 'level up' in professions without ever having to fire a shot. The galaxy is yours to immerse yourself in as you see fit.

But the thing is - if you don't enjoy flying around in space, this is the majority of the game. You will do a lot of jumps. You can setup auto-pilots to fly around and land/launch, but if that's the way you're going this game will feel incredibly boring. The fun lies in the little moments: most of your game is spent flying around, getting stuff so you can... fly around more. If that isn't for you, Elite is not the type of game you are going to have fun in.

You're also going to have to delve deep into community-made tools and sites to help you navigate the galaxy. Be prepared for lots of searches on 'how do I x?' 'what is y?' - the community is fantastically helpful and provides a ton of useful information that would otherwise be obtuse or obfuscated in the game.

If you're looking for a game to get stuck into, and one that you're willing to take a deep breath and work through the initial teething issues, Elite is the game for you. 

So imagine a calm blue ocean, grit your teeth and push through the initial 'wtf is this' stages, because once Elite opens up - oh boy, there ain't nothing else like it.

Elite has been good while it lasted.

So many stuff to see and experience. All those interesting ships and modules. Curious missions and Background Simulations. If you are thinking of buying, you won't be disappointed in these first couple of hours.



But the downside, if you choose to pursue a goal like a fully engineered ship, is an ever eternal job. There comes a point when the tinted glasses wears off and the fun turns into monotony. You will reach a point pretty quick where you need a lot of credits. This is when you, unfortunately, google and discover so many legitimate ways to earn enough to buy the next best ship. Posts where mining Low Temperature Diamonds could net you large sums of credits, bounty hunting is roughly 10x worst at money making, trading and passenger is the relatively fast, middle ground. [b]Nerfed.[/b]

Find a hotspot, mine, then re-join into the game, mine the respawned hotspot. Now there is a [b]shared global 6 hours[/b] respawn timer to any main asteroid and a [b]local 2 hours[/b] for any minor ones. Solution: use third party website to find a pristine ring of untouched materials.

Bounty hunting was really worthless. Imagine making 10k per bounty but your mining is doing 100k+ [b]per material[/b]. They have buffed it, but it is on par as every other money makers as of 2021, which is very average.

If the ship is wrecked one way or another, you have to pay 5% of the total ship cost. In the example above, the total is 384 million and the minimum way to get it back is paying 19.2 million credits. If you cannot pay the amount in that very specific screen, that 7 days of grind means nothing and have to start with the starter ship again.

You own a Carrier? You better pay that millions of credits every week or it will become decommissioned. You cannot pay during the decommission period? Good bye to your billion credit Carrier.

Then there is that very inane and insane grind. You want to hunt Xenos, but you have to travel far to an alien site and do some grind and re-login strategy to get enough materials to buy an anti-xeno module. Engineers eat your resources to play some mini "spin the wheel" game where RNG decides if your upgrade progress is a lot or very little. For every single module, [b]per upgrade rank[/b]. Same goes for all ranking in game that has ships or weapons locked behind a faction. Sometimes even access to a solar system. [b]Especially Earth's solar system[/b].




If you still do go ahead and buy the game, I do hope you enjoy it while it last. Elite do have the potential to beat all space sim in the category. But the only thing holding it back is the developers and the company themselves. This has been a problem since 2016, after the release of Horizons.

MY TAKE AWAY***
-SOUNDS: The game is beautiful, stunning graphics and don't even get me started on the sounds. Ok, you got me started on the sounds. 
-GRAPHICS: like I said beautiful, even on a low-end graphics card (I've used a GTX750 and moved on to an RTX Super 2060) light visuals map well even though RTX isn't supported, our universe is gorgeous and they did a great job at recreating the stunning visuals. Ships look great and the perspective of how MASSIVE everything is (even other ships) cannot be described until you are staring at a behemoth of a ship passing by your little starting fighter.
-CONTROLS: I used an Xbox one controller, the game throws you into a tutorial right off the bat and doesn't teach much simply because you don't know the keymapping until you get a chance to go into the settings. That being said, this game is a glorious FLIGHT SIM meaning 300,000 controls available for mapping to Game Controllers, Mouse/Keyboard, Joysticks, Tobii gestures, pedals, anything. Spend 30 minutes mapping the keys and testing some things right off the bat. Then go do some missions to get the hang of what controls you use the most and spend another 30 minutes fine-tuning the mapping. You will be much happier, the alternative is frustration or simply never using certain features. My preferred set up would be two joysticks with plenty of side buttons and a set of 6 Axis pedals. The Xbox controller works just fine otherwise. 
-GAME FEATURES/GAMEPLAY: The game is a flight sim. The entire game is a solid foundation to one day become any game built upon this foundation (think GTA V, racing, fps, campaign story, multiplayer shenanigans, etc) but right now it is simply (said lightly here) a MASSIVE universe mapped the best they could do off of our real universe that takes years (depending on your ship/set up) to get across the whole thing (seriously as of writing this no one has made it across the universe yet.) WHAT IS IN THE GAME WORLD? Solar systems with space stations and AI outlaws, Civilians, Planetary stations, and mineable asteroid belts. That's it. There are a few easter eggs just for visuals, like the Voyager 1 in our Solar system. Oh, also some aliens deep in space (just some bad AI characters with cool 'ships') WHAT CAN YOU DO IN THE GAME? You start in a space station with a starter ship. There is a universal currency used to purchase upgrades for your ship, supplies, and new ships. YOU CAN NEVER LEAVE YOUR SHIP. there is no walking around, the closest you can get is a planetary rover or small deployable fighter ship. So all you can do is what your ship is capable of doing. This means equipping weapons (lasers, machine guns, rockets) and fighting some baddies or some civilians, equipping mining equipment to blast asteroids and send your limpet ai drones to go scoop up the valuable minerals to make some money, equipping cargo holds and playing the market between the space stations by selling minerals/etc between systems, or passenger-holds to do the same. There are several factions you dedicate yourself to and rank up in doing missions involving the only things your ship is capable of which will unlock new ships for you and permits to visit solar systems (like SOL). Overall the gameplay is lackluster after trying everything once, I ended up spending most of my time grinding asteroid belts for cash, or fighting outlaws with friends. ONE DAY THIS GAME will have some real game like features; until then it's a fantastic, visually-stunning flight simulator with the perfect foundation to become any game in the future. 

PROS: Visuals A++, Audio A+++, Control customization A+++,  Flying A+++. Did i say audio?

CONS: Lacking a story to captivate you, lacking real gamified or competitive features to keep things fun. Once you master flying you've really hit the ceiling of the skill level required to do anything. Flying and sightseeing is the main game. Seeing how far you can travel and how expensive your ship is seems to be the end goal for this game as of right now.

TL;DR: You are always in a space vehicle, there is no walking around. The Universe is based on our own and is MASSIVE. Space stations, roving ai space ships, and mining asteroids is about all there is to do aside from sightseeing our universe. Flying is fantastic and is the main enjoyment in this game. 
You would love this game if you enjoy looking at space and flying simulators, you would hate this game if you're looking for actual gameplay/mission progression.

Oh, and the sounds are fantastic. Did I say that?

It took me a while to figure out exactly what Elite Dangerous is.  I know now that it's a sci-fi space simulation in the style of an open world, vaguely sandboxy MMO, with some old-school elements.

Just like in some of the oldest MMOs, this is a world for you to partake in, not a theme park built for your personal amusement.  The goal is whatever you decide it is, and there are numerous aspects of the game which place realism before entertainment.  Most notably, sometimes you'll be flying in a straight line for a good chunk of time, because space is big.  What do you do during this time?  Just what your character would do as the pilot--listen to something, read something, but keep half an eye on the situation because surprises can and do happen during those flights.

When not traveling, you'll be fully engaged in the gameplay.  Whether combat, exploration, trading, mining, or otherwise, it's up to you how you'll participate.  The game is very good at letting you engage with what you want, and ignore what you don't.  For one player this may be a space combat simulator, for another it's a calm and quiet deep space exploration game, for another it may be a big-picture strategic effort to expand the territory of their chosen political entity.

The flexible design is demonstrated in the current big event, the Thargoid invasion.  While most would assume that an alien invasion calls for combat ships, Elite gives you the freedom to help in many ways.  Trading ships can bring supplies to the front, passenger vessels are perfectly suited to evacuate refugees from damaged stations, and all of this helps in the overall war effort to save human space.  If you're not interested, you can ignore the invasion entirely.

The amount of choice involved in ship design is staggering.  Dozens of slots to fill with a wide variety of options, each of which is further customizable through engineering.  Little details matter as well--for example, a point defense turret mounted on the top of your ship won't be able to shoot down missiles coming at you from below.

With the Odyssey expansion, on foot FPS-style gameplay is added.  Your options here range from the structured 12v12 point-controlling matches found in conflict zones to Deus Ex style stealth missions, or unstructured looting and pillaging of settlements if that's what you prefer.  And for the deep space explorers, the new ability to catalogue alien flora on planet surfaces is added.  Character progression on foot is largely separate from that of ship content, but all of your activity on foot or in ship feeds into the same background political-economic simulation that all players participate in.

There is a lot of lore to dig in to, if you wish.  Or you can ignore it if not, as with most other aspects of the game.

Now the (potential) negatives, because this game is certainly not for everyone.

This game does not hold your hand, and it's quite overwhelming at first.  For every new thing you do, you'll be totally lost.  You will not be given an endless series of quests that guide you through the entire game, as found in modern MMOs.  However, there are ample resources available to teach you, whether the built-in tutorials (which are easy to miss in the menus) or Youtube videos made by players.  Once you get a handle on Elite, it becomes a familiar and comfortable world to take part in.

Some aspects of flying your ship can be automated away with optional modules, if you choose, but even having done so the flight model is more complex than you'll find in most non-flight-sim games.  Flying itself is a skill to be learned, and unless you go pure Odyssey and never board your ship, it is one you will have to learn.

The game can be grindy if you make it so.  This isn't a game that will give you everything within a few days, or weeks.  I recommend pursuing multiple goals at once--repetitive grinding after a single one is just self-inflicted punishment.  If you can't be happy until you're at the top, if you can't enjoy the journey, this game is not for you.

There are almost no rules in terms of player behavior.  Other players may attack you for any or no reason.  You can choose to play only with friends, or in solo mode (in which you will encounter only NPCs, but still participate in the shared political-economic simulation), or you can block specific players ensuring you'll never instance with them again.  Griefers are out there, but mostly confined to specific high-popularity locations.

There are bugs.  I've encountered numerous UI issues, but none that I couldn't work around.  There are several things that won't update in a timely manner and require a quick relog to fix.  There is a strange bug with the handheld guns that sometimes results in zero recoil.  One specific mission type is just straight up broken and impossible sometimes.  All of these issues apparently have been around for quite some time, and the developers don't seem to be very good about fixing them.

(Note, I've probably put another 200+ hours into this game as whatever the counter says, because ED and Horizons used to be separate clients in Steam)

This game gets so many things right. When you first start, there's a an entire GALAXY for you to explore.  In VR, it's everything you'll ever want.  You can be a pirate, you can be a miner, an explorer, a trader, or even a bounty hunter.  You'll spend one or two hundred hours having some of the most amazing fun exploring all of the different systems.

Yes, you read that correctly, one or two hundred hours.  That fully encompasses the learning curve for this game, across all of the things you can do, and the curve it takes to earn your way into a mid or high-tier ship.

But THAT is when the honeymoon ends.

That is when you discover that Elite is a game that covers an entire galaxy, and is exactly one inch deep (or less) across all of it.  You'll notice that your HUD contains the exact same data in three different spots, while jumping.  You'll see that updates are focused on PvP balance, and new features, and not fixing broken mission systems.  You'll realize that the seemingly detailed background simulation doesn't spawn ships to move those goods.  It'll dawn that you can't effectively interact with npcs AT ALL.  You'll outgun hordes of npcs.  You will involuntarily become an outlaw by simply *trying* to bounty hunt if a stray shot so much as looks at a system-authority vessel.  You will scream in frustration at paying a $20M rebuy because someone killed you - and got only a couple thousand credit bounty - which they cleared by using the starting ship to have cops kill them. You will realize that one ship, the Anaconda, can do every single role in the game better and cheaper than yours.  You will realize mining, exploring, and everything that isn't Combat/PvP hasn't had an update...ever.  You will probably even join the forums, and reddit, and see YEARS of requests to fix broken features, implement promised ones, etc....

But, most of all....

YOU

WILL

GRIND.

You'll grind for the ability to buy a ship, upgrade a ship, be able to not die *instantly* in pvp.  You'll spend an hour flying to Hutton Orbital for no good reason, and you'll come to realize that this game simply doesn't respect your time.  You will find that the average play session consists of:
<game>
I'd like to do fun thing X!

But first, I have to fly to Y, and buy/refit my ship. (+30 min)

Then, I need to LEAVE THE GAME to use an external tool to find a place to do X! (+10min)

Now, I need to actually get to location X, and have fun! (+30min)

Okay, now that I'm here, need to cruise to the location to do that fun thing! (+5 min)

Great, now that I'm here! I can finally, after over an hour, have fun....

FIVE MINUTES LATER:

Welp, (cargo full, ship destroyed, or event over) that was....fun?
</game>

Then, you'll put the game down, only to peek in after a major update to see if they've fixed it yet.  At this point, the Commanders added "multi-crew" (read: "multi-pew"), which is really combat-only changes, and SELFIES!

My advice, pick it up on sale, only. But do not over-invest your time.  Revel in being in a "little" ship. Don't get "rich".  Just play with friends, on mobius (a pve only group) or a private group, and just have fun.  Because there is no endgame, only grind. There is no depth, only more bolt-on features that will be abandoned soon after release.

EDIT #1:  While I didn't mean to poo-poo the idea of pvp. Someone has commented that I must suck at it or have never tried it. I assure you, I have. I'm not interested in risking a 5-20Mcr rebuy on my ship (which represents many hours of work) so that some no-lifer can blow up my ship.  CQC has better combat mechanics, and will do just fine (OH WAIT! CQC was abandoned just like every other released feature... so nyah!) 

Besides... who wants to spend weeks scanning T-9s in outbreak systems just to get access to a single engineer? 
...Just to turn around and collect several (nonsensical) fetch-quest for shopping-lists worth of stuff to fulfill a recipe.
...to roll some dice and hope RNGesus smiles on you?  
...Just to be able to keep up with the current pvp meta?
...which is bound to change next patch?
If you've answered "yes" to the above: you're a fan of shameless grinding! I've better ways to spend my time.  Which brings me to....

I'm sorry, but hours spent in game doesn't equal value. (Especially when 90% of that time is spent in loading screens or waiting for something. If I can watch netflix while I play, am I really playing?)  If you don't agree, that's your perogative, but Elite presents itself as an MMO, and as a simulator.  It's failing on both fronts. That's why it gets a thumbs down.  This game is capable of more, but it's pushing new features instead of fixing its flaws - and that's bad. Real bad.

tl;dr 

This game is like the TV series "LOST". At the beginning, it's OMG FREAKING AWESOME!!! But, with every new addition, every new feature, every opened plotline, it slowly descends....until you wonder when your beloved surroundings morphed into a complete shit-show without you noticing until well-after it's too late, and you're so invested that you just can't walk away because, someday, they are going to wrap-up at least one of those plot lines....

...but someday never arrives.

A lot of people complain that there isn't a story or much to do. Personally I just like setting up my joysticks, popping on my VR headset and mining/space trucking for hours while listening to podcasts. If you really want to go nuts you can use something like OVR Toolbox to drop a Netflix window into your cockpit.

Also I only play in private groups. The last thing I need is to have my chill ruined by some troll in open play.

TLDR; Not recommending for one reason: The most progress I've made in this game were some of the darkest and worst experiences of gaming in my life where I sacrificed health and a significant amount of personal time for slight gains in-game. The average person will literally hate everything about this game but only know about 10hrs in, after the refund limit, while the addiction-prone person will get hooked.

Considering I have 600+ hrs in the game, I can honestly say I got my moneys worth. I've been to the center, I have the biggest ships (Duval rep), I have two fully engineered PvP ships, fully engineered explorer, miner, etc, so I've "accomplished" some stuff over that time.

But, a big but.

Only a very small fraction of those hours are really enjoyable. The rest were really just me having been crushed by boredom and the game's grind itself and just sitting the ship looking at shit or leaving the game open while I watch Youtube vids.

This games physics are really incredible, the flight is incredible, the cockpit, ship and most exploration/celestial body visuals are incredible. That's essentially where it stops. Even while the physics are rooted in reality (except no orbits, honestly wtf), the application of research, exploration etc, has no basis in reality so I can't say the "scientific" aspect of this game is up to snuff.

If you are a flight simmer and you enjoy things like:
 - Practicing landing a jet for no reason
 - Flying from your city to another city for no reason
 - Learning how a weapon system works for no reason

If you are a grinder and enjoy things like:
 - Doing the same thing for LEGIT 18hrs straight with no change or difference to sound, visuals, experience, hand input, etc
 - Doing the same mission type that has literally 0 actual experience change other than a slight different text dialogue, thousands, and i mean thousands of times
 - Finding ways to make credits to increase your fleet with the community for the devs to go squash it right after (I'm looking at you Conflict Zones, how could you nerf those Frontier? I quit the game when you did that)
 - Having large updates pushed to further dates (not the end of the world, but I won't even touch the game until the on-planet visual improvements)

Then you'll like this game. It's def more for the grinder or simmer than the average gamer. And once you become hooked you become SUPER disappointed and I'll even wager a quite depressed and unhealthy while you go through the grind.
